article_title: eMINTS Comprehensive Program
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2020). eMINTS Comprehensive Program Intervention Report │ Teacher Excellence Topic Area. NCEE WWC 2020-011. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Four-component design of eMINTS: sequenced professional development, coaching, technology integration, and online resources
description: The report enumerates four key components of eMINTS. Sequenced professional development delivers "approximately 140 hours of professional development focused on integrating technology into the classroom and developing lessons that use inquiry-based learning" over 2 or more years. Coaching provides one-on-one classroom sessions by instructional specialists plus group coaching to build school learning communities. Technology integration supports inquiry-based instruction, differentiated learning, and assessment. Online resources supply an eMINTS portal with assessments, lesson plans, example classroom websites, and online courses.
requirements: Trained instructional specialists to deliver professional development and coaching
Individual student access to Internet-connected computers or tablets for technology integration
constraints: A shorter version, eMINTS4All, includes fewer professional development sessions and coaching visits
target_learning_goals: Inquiry-based, technology-supported instruction
Classroom assessment and classroom management
Building a community of learning in schools
examples: At the end of the first year, teachers develop a classroom website with the help of the instructional specialist as a resource for students and their families
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2020). eMINTS Comprehensive Program Intervention Report │ Teacher Excellence Topic Area. NCEE WWC 2020-011. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/705

article_title: eMINTS
citation: eMINTS (enhancing Missouri's Instructional Networked Teaching Strategies): Program description and evidence summary. (2023). Evidence for ESSA. https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Build principal leadership and observation capacity alongside teacher professional development when implementing an instructional improvement program
description: eMINTS treats implementation leadership as part of the intervention itself: "The model also has a strong emphasis on helping principals understand and lead the program implementation and carry out teacher observations to support teachers' instructional performance." Professional development is thus directed not only at teachers but at principals and technology coordinators, so school leaders can understand, lead, and monitor the program rather than merely host it.
requirements: Principals receive professional development to understand and lead program implementation
Principals conduct teacher observations to support instructional performance
target_learning_goals: program implementation leadership
instructional quality through observation and support
examples: Professional development is provided to principals, technology coordinators, and classroom teachers in middle schools.
key_sources: eMINTS (enhancing Missouri's Instructional Networked Teaching Strategies): Program description and evidence summary. (2023). Evidence for ESSA. https://www.evidenceforessa.org

article_title: Educating for Democracy
citation: Susan E. Sporte and Joseph E. Kahne. (2007). Educating for Democracy: Lessons from Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research Research Brief. http://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: Embed civic best practices across the curriculum rather than relying on required civics courses
description: The article concludes that requiring courses in American Government may help but will not guarantee the learning opportunities found most important. Instead, "policymakers and educators need to look for ways to embed 'best practices' into classrooms by highlighting the importance of these practices and related civic outcomes, as well as through curriculum and professional development opportunities." These practices—service learning, open discussion of controversial issues, and community problem solving—can take place in any class, including art, English, or science.
requirements: Classroom practices must actually occur in classrooms; merely offering a civics or government course is not enough, since prior studies assessing only course offering found no relationship.
constraints: The authors note more than one-third of Chicago students reported not discussing issues they care about in any class over the year, showing these practices are not yet widespread.
target_learning_goals: commitment to civic participation
community problem solving
examples: An art teacher at Excel Academy had students investigate and reflect on school violence and create a poster campaign promoting peace; an English teacher at Lakeview High School held open discussions in which students questioned him, each other, and sources; an environmental science class at the School of Social Justice studied electrical power generation and local environmental justice issues.
key_sources: Susan E. Sporte and Joseph E. Kahne. (2007). Educating for Democracy: Lessons from Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research Research Brief. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/educating-democracy-lessons-chicago

article_title: Measuring student reading comprehension performance: Considerations of accuracy, equity, and engagement by embedding comprehension items within reading passages
citation: Guerreiro, M., & Johnson, J. (2022). Measuring student reading comprehension performance: Considerations of accuracy, equity, and engagement by embedding comprehension items within reading passages. Practical Assessment, Research, and Evaluation, 27.
title: Embed comprehension items throughout reading passages to reduce extraneous measurement barriers
description: This principle holds that reading comprehension assessments should present items throughout a passage rather than only at its conclusion, because end-of-passage formats may inadvertently measure extraneous constructs. The article argues embedding achieves "a more precise measure of reading comprehension by removing barriers for students to demonstrate their understanding."
requirements: Assessment items must remain related to the passage content
constraints: Evidence is limited to reading comprehension assessment contexts
target_learners: K-12 students taking reading comprehension assessments
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of reading comprehension
examples: The study compared embedded-item passages with traditional end-of-passage item placement and found a significant impact on measured achievement.

article_title: Pause, Collect, Reflect Protocol
citation: Pause, Collect, Reflect Protocol. (2026). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Embed portfolio pauses into existing classroom structures
description: Portfolio routines work best when integrated into the classroom's existing rhythms rather than added on. The guide instructs educators to integrate the pause "directly into your existing classroom structures so it feels like a natural part of the learning cycle rather than an afterthought." It also recommends clearly communicating the purpose of the collection and reflection processes to students and families early.
requirements: Early communication of the portfolio purpose to students and families
Existing classroom structures into which the routine can be integrated
target_learning_goals: Sustained portfolio curation and reflection as part of classroom culture
examples: The guide suggests using the protocol in professional learning communities, faculty meetings, or leadership retreats to plan implementation.

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Saga Math
citation: Saga Math (Evidence Summary). (2020). Evidence for ESSA program evidence summary. https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Embedded high-dosage tutoring pattern: small ratios, in-schedule sessions, and classroom-aligned sequencing
description: The Saga approach instantiates a high-dosage tutoring design in which tutoring is "embedded in students' regular school schedules", occurs at least three times weekly for 90 minutes, uses small tutor-to-student ratios (1:2 to 1:4 traditional; up to 1:8 blended with ALEKS), and trails classroom instruction by 2-3 days to reinforce learning and address gaps. Program strategies are adjusted using assessment data, observations, survey feedback, and progress-monitoring tools.
requirements: Minimum three sessions per week totaling 90 minutes, scheduled within the school day
Small tutor-to-student ratios per session (3-8 students depending on model)
Weekly alignment meetings between tutor supervisors and primary math teachers
constraints: Must remain supplemental so it does not displace Tier 1 instruction or other responsibilities
target_learners: High school students at risk of dropping out in high-poverty schools
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement, course grades, and course passing
examples: The blended model has 9th grade students spend every other day with a tutor for an hour at a 2-students-to-1-tutor ratio, with off days on computer-assisted learning

article_title: Researching Digital Learning Platforms: Foundations, Methods, and Policy Recommendations
citation: Wei, X., Roschelle, J., Pautz Stephenson, S. & Wortman, A. (2025). Researching digital learning platforms: Foundations, methods, and policy recommendations. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/257
title: Embedded experimental designs: randomized experiments and structured comparisons run inside DLPs during authentic learning
description: This pattern describes embedding interventions directly within platform infrastructure—modifying problem formats, feedback types, or visual scaffolds—and observing effects during authentic learning activities. The paper highlights several variants: RCTs, A/B testing (e.g., E-TRIALS in ASSISTments), factorial designs (Terracotta), and adaptive learning interventions. As the authors state, 'One important affordance of some DLPs is the ability to conduct randomized experiments or structured comparisons at scale.'
requirements: Platform infrastructure must allow content modification or experimental embedding; researchers must assess the platform's flexibility in advance, and fidelity monitoring tools such as teacher dashboards and backend logs are essential
constraints: Not all DLPs permit experimental embedding (e.g., Khan Academy provides limited backend access); IRB and district approvals, implementation fidelity, generalizability across platforms and domains, and logistical coordination with school calendars are stated challenges
target_learners: Middle school, medical, and online learners using DLPs in authentic settings
target_learning_goals: Causal evaluation of instructional design features such as feedback timing, worked examples, and adaptive item selection
examples: The paper cites ASSISTments RCTs (Feng et al., 2023; Smith et al., 2022), a Kahoot! RCT in medical education, ASSISTments E-TRIALS A/B testing, and Terracotta factorial designs
key_sources: Wei, X., Roschelle, J., Pautz Stephenson, S. & Wortman, A. (2025). Researching digital learning platforms: Foundations, methods, and policy recommendations. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/257

article_title: Making Dual Enrollment Work: Solving the Access-Success Paradox with OUSD's Point Person Model
citation: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Roldan-Rueda, D., & Blanchard, A. (2026). Making dual enrollment work: Solving the access–success paradox with OUSD’s point person model. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Embedded two-adult classroom: college instruction delivered on the high school campus with a familiar school-based adult present
description: OUSD delivers college courses on high school campuses during the school day, taught by Peralta instructors with an OUSD point person present—a dynamic some educators describe as team teaching. This "college comes to you" approach removes transportation barriers and integrates dual enrollment into students' daily schedules. During instruction the point person's presence provides students continuity and familiarity and gives instructors local knowledge and classroom management support. Point people scaffold students' agency, encouraging them to move from asking the point person questions to approaching the college instructor directly.
requirements: A funded point person (teaching line, second prep, assigned duty, or floating staff) assigned to each section, plus partnership agreements between district and college
constraints: Point person engagement varies from active classroom management to a less active but available presence; the model depends on Peralta instructors traveling to high school campuses
target_learners: High school students taking college courses, including students intimidated by or uncertain about approaching college instructors
target_learning_goals: Engagement with college-level instruction and development of student agency and confidence
examples: At one school students meet the Peralta instructor on Tuesdays and Fridays for 90-minute blocks; on Wednesdays the point person leads a shorter session for asynchronous work, quizzes, and project support.
key_sources: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Roldan-Rueda, D., & Blanchard, A. (2026). Making dual enrollment work: Solving the access–success paradox with OUSD’s point person model. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED681373

article_title: If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover
citation: Davis Dixon, Ashley Griffin, and Mark Teoh. (2019). If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover. The Education Trust & Teach Plus. https://edtrust.org
title: Empower and invest in teachers through responsive professional development, leadership pathways, and classroom autonomy
description: School leaders retain teachers of color by securing growth resources, funding conference attendance, embracing distributive leadership, and allowing discretion over materials and course content. One principal scrapped planned PD to "make sure that we're feeding our staff and we're giving them what they want," showing teachers their feedback is valued and implemented. The report states the space to advocate on students' behalf "makes it more likely a teacher will stay."
requirements: Principals must budget for professional development and be willing to cede control over aspects of schooling, including purchasing culturally relevant materials teachers request.
target_learning_goals: Teacher retention, professional growth, instructional autonomy
examples: Principals sent groups of teachers to the Black Male Educators' Convening in Philadelphia and bought class sets of The Hate U Give and Pushout at teachers' request.

article_title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy and Sustainable Development: An Ethical Governance and Development Goals Framework
citation: Md. Masudul Islam, Mirza Niaz Morshed, Md. Shafiqul Islam. (2025). Artificial Intelligence Literacy and Sustainable Development: An Ethical Governance and Development Goals Framework. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-7643-5420
title: Embed AI literacy competencies into curricula, institutional policies, and governance mechanisms
description: The article's central design recommendation is to treat AI literacy as a governance capacity rather than only a classroom outcome, embedding it across education and policy systems. As stated in the abstract: "The study proposed to embed literacy -based competencies into curricula, institutional policies, and governance mechanisms to accelerate equitable and responsible progress toward sustainable development goals." This follows from the finding that technical awareness alone is insufficient without ethical and governance readiness.
requirements: Foundational AIRE levels (Recognize, Comprehend, Apply) integrated into undergraduate and early-stage learning environments, with higher tiers addressed through professional development and knowledge management practices
constraints: Prevailing regulatory approaches remain largely compliance-oriented, prioritizing technical control over the cultivation of public understanding, which the article identifies as a barrier
target_learners: learners, educators, policymakers, and institutions across national education and governance systems
target_learning_goals: ethical decision-making, responsible AI use, and SDG-aligned governance capacity
examples: The article proposes measurable indicators such as accessibility compliance, bias gaps, and traceability metrics adapted from established SDG indicators to link literacy initiatives with sustainable development outcomes

article_title: AIfred: Augmented Learning through Functional Robotic Embodiment at the Desk
citation: Gregorio Orlando, Milan Groshev, Eduardo Castelló Ferrer. (2026). AIfred: Augmented Learning through Functional Robotic Embodiment at the Desk. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38737
title: Embed AI guidance physically within the learner's workspace when guidance and task share a spatial frame
description: The article recommends delivering AI assistance directly into the physical workspace rather than on a separate screen, because projected guidance keeps digital content aligned with handwritten work and avoids context switching. The authors state that "co-locating guidance matters most when the instructions and the task share a unified spatial frame", and that robot-mediated projection is "not a general-purpose replacement for screen-based assistance, but a targeted one". The principle is instantiated by AIfred's robot-mediated projection of task-relevant guidance next to physical work materials.
requirements: A projection or in-situ display mechanism capable of placing generated guidance at the location of the physical work
Perception of the user's physical task context so generated content is task-relevant
constraints: Symbolic content that can be read from a screen and reproduced on paper gains less from co-location; the benefit concentrates in spatial tasks such as drawing
Screen-based assistance remained faster for repeated revisions in the image-generation task
target_learners: adult learners and creative practitioners doing desk-based work
target_learning_goals: short-term learning transfer of practiced reasoning
drawing and creative output quality
examples: AIfred projected hints, formulas, and reasoning cues next to math work, and projected reference images and tutorials directly onto the learner's paper during drawing
key_sources: Gregorio Orlando, Milan Groshev, Eduardo Castelló Ferrer. (2026). AIfred: Augmented Learning through Functional Robotic Embodiment at the Desk. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38737

article_title: Confident yet Concerned: Inconsistencies in Computing Students'' Attitudes on Cybersecurity
citation: Adama, V., Biddle, R., Arachchilage, N., & Lottridge, D. (2026). Confident yet Concerned: Inconsistencies in Computing Students' Attitudes on Cybersecurity. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18541
title: Emerging attitude of resignation toward cybersecurity, analogous to digital resignation and privacy cynicism
description: The article proposes, as future work, an attitude of resignation specific to cybersecurity, drawing on Draper and Turow's "digital resignation" and Hoffmann et al.'s "privacy cynicism", defined as "an attitude of uncertainty, powerlessness and mistrust towards the handling of personal data by online services, rendering privacy protection behaviour subjectively futile". Because the study observed interest in cybersecurity alongside a lack of confidence and self-efficacy, the authors suggest resignation may be emerging for security as it has for privacy.
requirements: Future research to test whether a cybersecurity-specific resignation attitude exists, as the authors state this would be important future work
constraints: The article offers this as a speculative suggestion from one survey, not a tested construct
target_learning_goals: cybersecurity awareness and protective behaviour
motivation to learn about cybersecurity
examples: The survey found one cluster less prepared, quite unconfident, and very interested in learning more, which the authors link to possible resignation

article_title: CogTax: A Four-Level Cognitive Taxonomy for Command-Line Computing Education
citation: Alonso-Carracedo, M., Fernandez-Boullon, R., Celard, P., Rodríguez-Martínez, F. J., & Otero-Cerdeira, L. (2026). CogTax: A Four-Level Cognitive Taxonomy for Command-Line Computing Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00140
title: Embedding-based semantic command representation with four pretrained models and four preprocessing strategies
description: A complementary representation encoding commands as dense vectors in a semantic space. The article defines it as follows: "An embedding model is a neural network trained to map arbitrary text to a fixed-length numeric vector, such that texts with similar meaning are mapped to nearby points in the resulting vector space." Four models are evaluated (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, all-mpnet-base-v2, multilingual-e5-small, BAAI/llm-embedder) under four preprocessing strategies: raw, normalized (replacing literals, paths, and numbers with placeholders), instruction-tuned (prepending a fixed classification prefix), and combined. Embeddings are language-agnostic by construction, supporting cross-language generalization.
requirements: Pretrained embedding models; choice of preprocessing strategy affects representation quality
constraints: Embeddings may miss structural complexity markers that have weak lexical correlates, per the article's framing of the two branches as complementary
target_learners: computing education researchers and instructors classifying commands
target_learning_goals: automatic assignment of taxonomy levels from command semantics

article_title: ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education
citation: Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti, Emanuele Frontoni. (2026). ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30662
title: Use embodied, multimodal avatars to make AI tutoring accessible to learners who struggle with text
description: The article argues that AI tutoring interfaces should move beyond text-only chatbots toward embodied multimodal virtual humans. It states that "speaking and gesturing avatars can benefit learners who struggle with text-based communication (e.g., young children or students with reading difficulties)" and can offer accessible modalities such as voice output, lip-reading support, or sign-language-capable avatars. The prototype operationalizes this with captions, adjustable speaking rate, simplified-language toggles, high-contrast UI, and lip-synchronized facial articulation.
requirements: Avatar facial articulation clear enough to avoid degrading comprehension during voice-based tutoring
Accessibility features (captions, speaking-rate control) exposed as first-class configuration options
constraints: The avatar was designed conservatively to remain legible on small screens while avoiding overly realistic features that may increase the risk of discomfort in some learners
target_learners: young children, students with reading difficulties, and learners with impairments
target_learning_goals: comprehensible, inclusive multimodal tutoring dialogue
examples: The client enforces clear turn-taking through listening/thinking/speaking states, and lip-sync is driven directly by the played audio

article_title: Decreasing Digital Distraction in College Students: Associated Online Learning Strategies Identified by Unsupervised
citation: Shi, H., Bi, R., Lin, X., & Dai, Y. (2025). Decreasing Digital Distraction in College Students: Associated Online Learning Strategies Identified by Unsupervised Data Mining Approaches. https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/P85S3
title: Embed explicit self-regulation training and self-control tools in online courses to foster lower digital distraction
description: The article recommends that educators build students' capacity to regulate attention in digital environments rather than only removing distractions. Because SRL strategies such as goal setting, environment structuring, and time management co-occurred most consistently with lower distraction, the authors advise that "educators can incorporate explicit training on self-control skills within course structures", including workshops on structured study schedules and self-control tools. This targets college students in online courses and the goal of maintaining focused engagement.
requirements: Educators need course structures that can host explicit training on self-control skills, such as workshops or modules on creating structured study schedules
constraints: The supporting evidence is associative and self-reported from one university sample; the article frames these as preliminary insights for future research, not tested interventions
target_learners: college students in synchronous online courses
target_learning_goals: maintaining focused attention and reducing off-task digital device use during online learning
examples: The article suggests embedding workshops or modules on creating structured study schedules and using online self-control tools like Pomodoro timers, task prioritization apps, and notification blockers, and designing synchronous sessions with real-time polls, Q&A sessions, and personalized communication.

article_title: Is hands-on learning still necessary in the age of AI? A thematic review
citation: Yu J, Liu L and Zhu Q (2026). Is hands-on learning still necessary in the age of AI? A thematic review. Front. Psychol. 17:1897168. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1897168
title: Process-oriented framework of expanded hands-on learning: Embodied Hands-on and Cognitive Hands-on
description: The review proposes that hands-on learning is expanding into two interrelated forms: Embodied Hands-on, based on the body, tools, and materials, and Cognitive Hands-on, based on language, judgement, and human–AI iteration. Both share a cycle of action, feedback, reflection, and refinement but rely on different sources of feedback and are not educationally equivalent. The framework emerged inductively from thematic analysis of 32 studies and is conceptual rather than empirically tested.
requirements: Learners must remain involved in action, feedback, reflection, and refinement for AI-supported activity to acquire the process characteristics of hands-on learning
constraints: The framework is conceptual and has not yet been empirically tested
There is insufficient evidence to show that the two forms can replace one another
target_learning_goals: creative thinking
design judgement
student agency
examples: The review synthesises prompting, generating, comparing, selecting, and revising as Cognitive Hands-on, and sketching, model making, and material experimentation as Embodied Hands-on
key_sources: Yu J, Liu L and Zhu Q (2026). Is hands-on learning still necessary in the age of AI? A thematic review. Front. Psychol. 17:1897168. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1897168

article_title: MathBuddy: Affective Math Tutoring
citation: Debanjana Kar, Leopold Böss, Dacia Braca, Sebastian Dennerlein, Nina Hubig, Philipp Wintersberger, and Yufang Hou. (2025). MathBuddy: A Multimodal System for Affective Math Tutoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19993
title: Map detected student affect to pedagogical moves: challenge positive/neutral students, motivate negative-affect students
description: MathBuddy operationalizes affective adaptation with a simple mapping rule: aggregated student emotion is reduced to Positive, Neutral, or Negative, and this state selects the tutor's pedagogical stance. As the authors state, "if the student is in a positive or neutral affective state, the student is challenged by MathBuddy, while a negative affective state causes the system to try to motivate the student." The rule is grounded in educational-psychology work on academic emotions and is delivered to the LLM tutor via system prompts. It turns continuous multimodal affect sensing into an actionable instructional decision at every conversational turn.
requirements: Reliable real-time emotion recognition from at least one modality (text or facial expression), aggregated into a Positive/Neutral/Negative state before each tutor response
constraints: The authors found that emotion information without education-theory grounding misguides smaller tutor models
The aggregation rule suppresses Neutral states, producing low Neutral recall (0.15) in the user study
target_learners: Mathematics learners in one-on-one tutoring with an LLM-based tutor
target_learning_goals: Math problem-solving with scaffolded guidance; maintaining engagement and motivation during tutoring
examples: In MathBuddy, the aggregated emotion from text (fine-tuned BERT classifier) and webcam facial expressions is mapped to primitives and injected into the tutor prompt, switching between challenge and motivate instructions

article_title: Rethinking AI-assisted writing instruction: feedback literacy scripts, calibration training, and student writing development
citation: Dai (2026). Rethinking AI-assisted writing instruction: feedback literacy scripts, calibration training, and student writing development. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1829268
title: Embed AI writing tools within instructional support structures rather than treating them merely as instant feedback sources
description: The article concludes that when AI writing tools are used in teaching, "they should not be treated merely as sources of instant feedback. Instead, they should be embedded within specific instructional support structures", so students develop independent judgment and self-regulated learning while using feedback. The rationale is that AI feedback does not automatically improve writing; its value depends on whether learners can evaluate, select, and transform feedback into revision decisions, as shown by the differentiated effects of FRAC and APCA.
requirements: Structured metacognitive support (feedback-processing scripts and/or calibration activities) must accompany AI feedback access
constraints: Evidence comes from one study of English majors at a single university; the article calls for testing in more diverse contexts
target_learners: undergraduate L2/EFL writers using generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: independent revision judgment
self-regulated writing development with AI support
examples: The study embedded AI feedback within FRAC decision sheets and APCA calibration logs across four writing task points rather than providing AI feedback alone

article_title: A Bottom-Up Taxonomy of Student Discourse with a Socratic AI Physics Tutor
citation: Syed Furqan Abbas Hashmi and N. Sanjay Rebello. (2026). A bottom-up taxonomy of student discourse with a Socratic AI physics tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07373
title: Emergent LLM coding plus embedding-based consolidation pipeline for large-scale student-discourse taxonomies
description: A two-step methodological framework, framed as the LLM analog of open coding in grounded theory, for converting large student-tutor transcript corpora into interpretable discourse categories. Step 1 asks an LLM coder to assign each turn an emergent free-text label using the previous four conversational turns as context, yielding 833 unique raw labels. Step 2 consolidates near-paraphrase labels via text embeddings, cosine distance, and agglomerative clustering with average linkage at a distance threshold of 0.40, followed by LLM-generated canonical category names, producing 357 consolidated categories. The approach follows computational grounded theory, letting categories be discovered rather than projected from a fixed codebook.
requirements: A context window of prior conversational turns (four turns was the smallest window recovering consistent labels for context-dependent moves); a distance-threshold sweep with human coherence inspection to select the clustering threshold; validation against expert coding.
constraints: Single-rater coherence judgments establish only face validity; rerunning consolidation with a different embedding model could shift category boundaries; specific category labels reflect the single mechanics problem context and will not transfer to tutors covering other content.
target_learners: introductory physics students interacting with AI tutors
target_learning_goals: characterizing student discourse and engagement with AI-tutor scaffolding
examples: The threshold 0.40 was selected as the largest setting at which ≥90% of inspected groups were judged coherent (47 of 50).
key_sources: Syed Furqan Abbas Hashmi and N. Sanjay Rebello. (2026). A bottom-up taxonomy of student discourse with a Socratic AI physics tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07373

article_title: From Classroom Design to Newsroom Practice: Assessment Intervention Designing GenAI
citation: Ngu, I. Y., & Weller, D. (2026). From Classroom Design to Newsroom Practice: Designing GenAI Assessment Intervention. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice. https://doi.org/10.53761/4281ht04
title: Embed GenAI into assessment through an ethical framework rather than banning it, to address integrity and professional values
description: Because GenAI both promises efficiencies and threatens academic integrity, authorship and core professional values, the article argues journalism educators should embed it into assessment deliberately. The intervention is "based on an ethical framework that embeds GenAI into undergraduate journalism assessment," scaffolding movement toward AI-integrated work and critical reflection rather than exclusion of the technology.
requirements: An ethical framework must guide which tasks are human-only and which are AI-integrated
constraints: Stated for journalism education, where authorship and professional core values are at stake
target_learning_goals: Ethical GenAI use in professional practice
examples: The paper's curriculum intervention embedded GenAI into undergraduate journalism assessment at a Malaysian campus

article_title: Enabling Multi-Agent Systems as Learning Designers: Applying Learning Sciences to AI Instructional Design
citation: Jiayi Wang, Ruiwei Xiao, Xinying Hou, John Stamper. (2025). Enabling Multi-Agent Systems as Learning Designers: Applying Learning Sciences to AI Instructional Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16659
title: Embed learning science principles directly into AI system architectures rather than relying on teacher prompting
description: The article argues that pedagogical expertise should shift "from the user's prompt to the LLM's internal architecture", because most teachers lack the time or expertise to encode pedagogical nuance into prompts. Its key contribution is "showing that embedding learning science principles directly into AI architectures is an effective way to produce pedagogically sound materials", bridging the prompting gap and moving AI from a content generator to a pedagogical partner.
requirements: Access to an LLM-based generation system whose architecture encodes a pedagogical framework, so teachers need not supply expert prompts themselves
constraints: The most effective architecture (MAS-CMD) carried substantially greater latency and token usage; the study evaluated designed activities, not classroom implementation, so there is no direct evidence of impact on student learning outcomes
target_learners: K-12 educators designing instruction with generative AI
target_learning_goals: Production of pedagogically sound, classroom-ready learning activities
examples: The study instantiated this principle by embedding the KLI framework into MAS-Roles and MAS-CMD and comparing them against a single-agent baseline simulating typical teacher prompts
key_sources: Jiayi Wang, Ruiwei Xiao, Xinying Hou, John Stamper. (2025). Enabling Multi-Agent Systems as Learning Designers: Applying Learning Sciences to AI Instructional Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16659

article_title: Can You Feel It? A Practical Guide to Emotional Micro-Interventions for Higher Education Teachers
citation: François PARLANT. (2025). Can You Feel It? A Practical Guide to Emotional Micro-Interventions for Higher Education Teachers (and Others). https://osf.io/tuw2a/overview
title: The Emotional Terrain Map: pairing negative emotional bottlenecks with their underlying narratives and target positive states
description: A diagnostic table mapping common negative emotional states in high-stakes learning against desired outcomes, serving as a tool for instructors to "name the emotion" they are witnessing and identify a pedagogical goal. Each row pairs a bottleneck (e.g., "Isolation/Shame") with its underlying narrative ("Everyone else gets it. I'm alone.") and a bridge state ("Camaraderie & Belonging"). It is the recognition step before selecting an intervention from the catalogs.
requirements: Effective intervention begins with recognition of the emotional state being witnessed
target_learners: Higher education instructors in skill-based courses
target_learning_goals: Diagnosing emotional bottlenecks to sustain engagement and persistence
examples: Frustration/Incompetence ('I can't do this. I'm not cut out for it.') maps to Resilience & Self-Efficacy ('I can troubleshoot and learn.')

article_title: \"If You Can't Dance Your Program, You Can't Write It\": Challenges and Implications for AI in Education
citation: Ronnie Videla, Simon Penny, Wendy Ross. (2025). 'If you can't dance your program, you can't write it': Challenges and Implications for AI in Education.
title: Embodied AI: a post-cognitivist framework grounding intelligent behavior and learning in physical interaction with the environment
description: The article advances Embodied AI as an epistemological and pedagogical framework contrasting with symbolic, disembodied AI. It states that "Embodied AI, which posits that intelligent behavior emerges from physical interactions with the environment, offers a compelling framework for understanding learning as an embodied process." It draws on post-cognitivist research "including frameworks such as 4E (embodied, enactive, embedded, extended) and SEEED (situated, embodied, enactive, embedded, distributed)", treating the body as the constitutive core of thought and knowledge as arising from organism–environment coupling rather than symbolic representation.
requirements: Educational design must integrate body, environment, and culture, recognizing that meaning emerges through interaction rather than isolated linguistic representation
constraints: The article notes its effective implementation requires material, institutional, and formative conditions that are often lacking in many educational settings
target_learners: learners across elementary through tertiary education
target_learning_goals: situated, creative, and critical understanding through embodied, sensorimotor engagement
examples: The article cites Brooks' subsumption architecture, in which layers of activity directly connect perception with action without centralized internal representations, as a precursor of this paradigm.
key_sources: Ronnie Videla, Simon Penny, Wendy Ross. (2025). 'If you can't dance your program, you can't write it': Challenges and Implications for AI in Education. https://doi.org/10.1145/3759257

article_title: Fostering self-regulated learning through adaptive learning technology: A differentiated perspective on the role of feedback
citation: Mathias Mejeh, Yvonne M. Fromm (2026). Fostering self-regulated learning through adaptive learning technology: A differentiated perspective on the role of feedback. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102394
title: Embed ALT feedback into instructional design and adapt feedback type to learners' cognitive, motivational, and emotional resources
description: The article recommends that adaptive learning technology not stand apart from teaching but be woven into course design with explicit expectations for feedback engagement, and that the type of feedback offered be matched to learners' current (meta-)cognitive, motivational, and emotional resources. Because comprehensive feedback did not necessarily improve SRL and some interactions were negative, timing and uptake are treated as key boundary conditions. The authors state that "ALTs should not be deployed as stand-alone feedback add-ons but should be embedded into instructional design through clear guidance on when and how students are expected to engage with feedback."
requirements: Instructors may need to actively support students' interpretation and use of ALT feedback and monitor whether feedback uptake occurs
constraints: Findings should be interpreted with caution due to the marginal significance of several effects; feedback effectiveness is context-dependent
target_learners: higher education students using adaptive learning technology
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning supported by personalized feedback
examples: In the study, feedback availability adapted to self-report thresholds while engagement remained voluntary, and the authors recommend instructors monitor whether such uptake actually occurs

article_title: Effective differentiation Practices:A systematic review and meta-analysis of studies on the cognitive effects of differentiation practices in primary education
citation: Deunk, M. I., Jacobse, A. E., de Boer, H., Doolaard, S., & Bosker, R. J. (2018). Effective differentiation Practices: A systematic review and meta-analysis of studies on the cognitive effects of differentiation practices in primary education. Educational Research Review, 24, 31-54. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2018.02.002
title: Embed differentiation practices in a broader educational context rather than relying on homogeneous ability grouping alone
description: This principle holds that differentiation should be implemented as part of a wider program or reform rather than as isolated grouping arrangements. The review's findings "emphasize that homogeneous ability grouping alone is not enough to guarantee differentiated instruction," which "stresses the importance of embedding differentiation practices in a broader educational context." Differentiation within a broader program showed small to moderate positive effects on performance.
requirements: Differentiation practices must be embedded in a broader educational context or program to be effective
constraints: Homogeneous ability grouping on its own does not guarantee differentiated instruction
target_learning_goals: language and math performance
examples: The meta-analysis found small to moderate positive effects when differentiation was used as part of a broader program or reform

article_title: Increasing the Problem-Solving Skills of Students with Developmental Disabilities Participating in General Education
citation: Agran, M., Blanchard, C., Wehmeyer, M., & Hughes, C. (2002). Increasing the Problem-Solving Skills of Students with Developmental Disabilities Participating in General Education. Remedial and Special Education, 23(5), 279-288. https://journals.sagepub.com
title: Embed problem-solving instruction into existing general education instructional programming
description: The study used an approach in which "problem solving was embedded or integrated into the existing instructional programming con ducted at that time," so the strategy fit the natural context of the classroom rather than requiring a separate intervention setting. This allowed instruction for students with developmental disabilities to occur entirely in general education content classes (science, life skills, and English) with class sizes of 22 to 35 students. All instruction was provided within those existing classes rather than in pull-out settings.
requirements: General education teachers must create and arrange opportunities within existing class activities for students to perform target behaviors and practice the strategy
constraints: The findings are specific to the target behaviors investigated; the authors state future research on other behaviors is needed
target_learners: students with developmental disabilities participating in general education
target_learning_goals: applying problem solving to classroom behaviors within the general curriculum
examples: Teachers created from three to five opportunities each day for the students to perform their target behaviors within their regular classes, with no peer support

article_title: Evolution and Revolution in Artificial Intelligence in Education
citation: Ido Roll & Ruth Wylie. (2016). Evolution and Revolution in Artificial Intelligence in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 582-599. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0110-3
title: Embed ILEs in context: treat the ILE as one technology in an ecosystem including teachers, curriculum, and culture
description: The article argues that instead of stand-alone plug-and-play environments, ILEs should be designed as one component of an ecosystem of classroom activities, instruction, and out-of-classroom activities, mindful of the intended environment from early design. Teachers should become active collaborators and participants, and ILEs should be embedded in cultural norms and broadened to informal and workplace contexts, since education is a socio-cultural phenomenon.
requirements: Future research should be mindful of the intended environment early in the design process.
constraints: The article found no examples of K-12 schools listed as affiliations on the reviewed papers; information about classroom context was so rarely provided it could not be analysed as a dimension.
target_learning_goals: authentic learning
culturally responsive learning
lifelong learning
examples: The Cognitive Tutor ecosystem introduces the technology together with a curriculum; Making History ports Second Temple history onto a Facebook timeline; the article reports 43 of 47 reviewed papers came from North America, Europe, and Oceania.

article_title: Emote aloud during learning with AutoTutor: Applying the Facial Action Coding System to cognitive–affective states during learning
citation: Scotty D. Craig, Sidney D'Mello, Amy Witherspoon, and Art Graesser. (2008). Emote aloud during learning with AutoTutor: Applying the Facial Action Coding System to cognitive/affective states during learning. Cognition and Emotion, 22(5), 777-788. https://doi.org/10.1080/02699930701516759
title: Emote-aloud procedure for on-line identification of affective states during learning
description: The emote-aloud procedure is a modification of the cognitive-science think-aloud method in which participants state aloud the affective state they are feeling while working on a learning task. Participants were given functional definitions of eight affective states drawn from Merriam-Webster OnLine and were video recorded while interacting with AutoTutor, verbalising states "without external prompts from the system or pressure from an experimenter in the room". The method "allows for on-line identification of affective states while working on a task, with minimal task interference" and proved useful for identifying points during learning where affective events occurred.
requirements: Participants must be given functional definitions of the target affective states prior to the session so that utterances are unambiguous
Video recording and labour-intensive coding (transcription, segmenting, interjudge reliability scoring) are needed, so samples are small
constraints: Not all participants are amenable to the procedure: 2 of 7 participants did not express affective states verbally
Unpredictable time samples prevent searching for stable sequential patterns of affective states
target_learning_goals: identification of affective states (anger, boredom, confusion, contempt, curiosity, disgust, eureka, frustration) during complex learning with an intelligent tutoring system
examples: Participants interacted with AutoTutor on computer literacy topics for 90 minutes, saying aloud any of the eight defined affective states whenever they experienced one; 10-second clips ending in an emote-aloud utterance were extracted for FACS coding.

article_title: Personalizing e-Learning. The Social Effects of Pedagogical Agents.
citation: Nicole C. Krämer & Gary Bente. (2010). Personalizing e-Learning. The Social Effects of Pedagogical Agents. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9123-x
title: Taxonomy of embodiment aspects and functions of nonverbal behavior for pedagogical agents
description: The article organizes embodiment into static aspects (the visual appearance of the virtual character) and dynamic aspects (nonverbal behavior such as movement, gesture, and facial displays), and proposes that nonverbal behavior serves distinct functions in instructional settings: a modeling function for demonstrating motor tasks, illustrative functions such as pointing gestures, a dialogue management function regulating turn-taking via gaze and backchanneling, and socio-emotional functions via immediacy cues like smiling and proximity. It further characterizes nonverbal communication by procedural character, context dependency, and production outside of awareness, arguing these attributes must shape agent implementation.
requirements: Implementing nonverbal behavior requires taking into account its procedural character, context dependency, and automaticity, as the article states all attributes must be considered
constraints: Current technical implementations remain far from matching the complexity and subtlety of real-life nonverbal behavior, per the article's conclusion
target_learners: e-learning students interacting with pedagogical agents
target_learning_goals: socio-emotional and relational outcomes as moderators or outcomes of learning
examples: The article suggests motion capture or time-series coded videotaped human behavior as routes to more natural agent movements

article_title: Investigating Epistemic Stances in Game Play with Data Mining
citation: Martinez-Garza, M. M., & Clark, D. B. (2017). Investigating Epistemic Stances in Game Play with Data Mining. International Journal of Gaming and Computer-Mediated Simulations, 9(3). https://doi.org/10.4018/IJGCMS.2017070101
title: Emulate evidence-centered design features (student model and evidence model) when applying learning analytics to game logs retrospectively
description: Because the full ECD framework cannot be applied retrospectively to existing game logs, the article recommends emulating its useful features: a student model operationalizing the hypothesized cognitive dynamics (here, the 2SM stances) and an evidence model mapping those dynamics onto observable log variables. The article states "the goal would be to emulate some useful features of ECD, such as the student model and the evidence model". This constrains latent variables, boosts interpretability, and pre-selects likely-significant observed variables.
requirements: A theory of the cognitive dynamics of play (here the 2SM) must be available to operationalize the student model before selecting log variables
constraints: The end result is not as robust as a full ECD evidentiary argument built into the assessment from the start
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of science content assessed through gameplay logs
examples: The student model defined Additive-Iterative and Solve-and-Debug modes; the evidence model selected response time, error rate, and actions per attempt as contrasting parameters

article_title: Empirically-Based Guidelines for the Design of Interactive Multimedia
citation: Innwoo Park and Michael J. Hannafin. (1993). Empirically-Based Guidelines for the Design of Interactive Multimedia. Educational Technology Research and Development, Vol. 41, No. 3, pp. 63-85. http://www.jstor.org/stable/30218388
title: Embed structural aids and generative activities so learners construct their own meaning
description: This principle holds that multimedia should support learners in selecting, organizing, and integrating content while prompting them to generate personal meaning. The article states that "Meaning is generated by the learner, not imposed on the learner through activities and examples," drawing on Wittrock's generative learning account. Structural organizers such as headings, lesson-structure introductions, summaries, and elaboration strategies should be embedded so learners integrate organized information into existing knowledge structures.
requirements: Structural aids must help learners identify and interpret relevant knowledge, processes guided more explicitly in traditional approaches
constraints: Learners' generated meaning may or may not parallel the designer's intended meaning
target_learning_goals: comprehension and integration of new knowledge with existing knowledge
examples: The article recommends introducing lesson structure, using headings to discriminate essential from supporting concepts, and summarizing key relationships among content

article_title: A meta-analytic examination of the instructional effectiveness of computer-based simulation games
citation: Traci Sitzmann. (2011). A Meta-Analytic Examination of the Instructional Effectiveness of Computer-Based Simulation Games. Personnel Psychology, 64, 489-528. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/journal/17446570
title: Embed simulation games as a supplement within a broader program of instruction rather than using them as standalone instruction
description: This principle holds that simulation games should be embedded in a program of instruction that includes other methods, because games alone rarely suffice for learning a topic. The meta-analysis found that "when simulation games were used as a supplement to other instructional methods, the simulation game group had higher knowledge levels than the comparison group (d = .51)", whereas standalone games yielded d = −.12 favoring the comparison group. The article reasons that when training utilizes a breadth of instructional methods, trainees having difficulty can review material through multiple methods to increase mastery, and debriefing sessions help transfer game learning to the job.
requirements: Other instructional methods must supplement the simulation game so trainees can review material through multiple channels
constraints: Standalone simulation games were counterproductive relative to comparison instruction (d = −.12)
target_learners: adult trainees in work-related and higher-education training programs
target_learning_goals: declarative and procedural knowledge and retention of trained material
examples: The meta-analysis classified studies by whether the simulation game was the sole instructional method or a supplement, and compared each category's effect size against comparison groups.
key_sources: Traci Sitzmann. (2011). A Meta-Analytic Examination of the Instructional Effectiveness of Computer-Based Simulation Games. Personnel Psychology, 64, 489-528. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/journal/17446570

article_title: Preschool interpersonal relationships predict kindergarten achievement: Mediated by gains in emotion knowledge
citation: Torres, M. M., Domitrovich, C. E., & Bierman, K. L. (2015). Preschool Interpersonal Relationships Predict Kindergarten Achievement: Mediated by Gains in Emotion Knowledge. Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.appdev.2015.04.008
title: Emotion knowledge as the developmental mediator linking early relationships to academic learning
description: The article advances a developmental model in which warm relationships with teachers and peers create opportunities to learn about emotions through explicit labeling and implicit modeling, and resulting emotion knowledge supports academic learning by promoting self-regulation of attention and emotion. The authors describe a related "process of emotion utilization, in which increasing emotion knowledge enables children to more efficiently channel emotional arousal into constructive thought and action". The study's SEM results are consistent with this model, though the authors stress the analyses do not test causal mechanisms.
requirements: Longitudinal designs controlling for cognitive ability and baseline emotion knowledge and achievement to test the mediation robustly
constraints: The article states the analyses are correlational and causal interpretations are unwarranted; unmeasured variables such as language or executive function may explain the associations
target_learners: economically-disadvantaged preschool children attending Head Start
target_learning_goals: emotion knowledge (identifying and recognizing emotions)
school readiness in emergent literacy and numeracy
examples: The study measured student-teacher closeness and positive peer interactions in fall, emotion knowledge at fall and spring, and achievement through kindergarten, testing the mediation with SEM

article_title: Knowledge is power: How conceptual knowledge transforms visual cognition
citation: Collins, Jessica A., & Olson, Ingrid R. (2014). Knowledge is Power: How Conceptual Knowledge Transforms Visual Cognition. Psychonomic bulletin & review. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-013-0564-3
title: Embodied cognition account: concepts are instantiated in the neural regions required for perception and action
description: The embodied account holds that "concepts are instantiated in the same neural regions required for specific types of perception and action." Support comes from neuroimaging showing sensory and motor areas are recruited during modality-specific semantic tasks (e.g., color knowledge activating left fusiform and lingual gyri), TMS studies showing causal roles of motor cortex in processing motion-related words, and behavioral interactions between motion perception and motion-language comprehension whose direction depends on stimulus saliency and integratability.
requirements: Modality-specific semantic processing that recruits the corresponding sensory or motor cortical systems
constraints: The review concludes the literature does not show embodiment is necessary for semantic understanding; behavioral effects may arise at response selection, and imaging activations may reflect spreading activation from amodal areas
target_learning_goals: understanding how semantic knowledge is neurally represented
examples: Retrieval of tactile information activates somatosensory, motor, and premotor areas; rTMS to hand-area M1 disrupts processing of hand-related words specifically
key_sources: Collins, Jessica A., & Olson, Ingrid R. (2014). Knowledge is Power: How Conceptual Knowledge Transforms Visual Cognition. Psychonomic bulletin & review. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-013-0564-3

article_title: Maternal emotional support but not cognitive support during problem-solving predicts increases in cognitive flexibility in early childhood
citation: Zeytinoglu, S., Calkins, S. D., & Leerkes, E. M. (2019). Maternal emotional support but not cognitive support during problem-solving predicts increases in cognitive flexibility in early childhood. International Journal of Behavioral Development, 43(1), 12-23. https://doi.org/10.1177/0165025418757706
title: Emotional support supports executive function growth via external regulation of arousal and opportunities to practice self-regulation
description: The article proposes a mechanism account in which emotionally supportive caregivers respond to children's needs warmly and encourage autonomy, thereby regulating children's physiological arousal during problem-solving. The article states that "emotionally supportive caregivers likely externally regulate the intensity of children’s physiological arousal and emotions," sustaining arousal levels conducive to coordinating executive functions. Children then internalize regulation strategies, practice executive skills more often, and develop positive attitudes toward cognitively challenging tasks, promoting growth of cognitive flexibility.
requirements: Caregiving observed in collaborative problem-solving contexts where children face cognitively challenging tasks
constraints: The account is the authors' theoretical interpretation; the study's longitudinal design does not test the proposed neural or arousal mechanisms directly
target_learners: children in early childhood (preschool to first grade, ages approximately 4-7)
target_learning_goals: growth of cognitive flexibility and executive functions during early childhood
examples: The study measured emotional support as observed emotional responsiveness, reversed intrusiveness, and reversed negativity during 7-minute mother-child board-game tasks at each wave

article_title: Which preschool mathematics competencies are most predictive of fifth grade achievement?
citation: Nguyen, T., Watts, T. W., Duncan, G. J., Clements, D. H., Sarama, J. S., Wolfe, C., & Spitler, M. E. (2016). Which Preschool Mathematics Competencies Are Most Predictive of Fifth Grade Achievement? Early Childhood Research Quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2016.02.003
title: Emphasize advanced counting competencies, not just rote verbal counting, in preschool mathematics instruction
description: The article concludes that early mathematics education should promote numeracy, specifically advanced counting: "our findings suggest that early mathematics education should promote the development of numeracy competencies, specifically advanced counting." Teachers should not restrict instruction to basic counting, since advanced counting skills include basic practice while developing cardinality, counting on, and conceptual subitizing. Recommended classroom activities include counting objects in arrays, comparing block-building quantities, and solving simple addition and subtraction problems in geometry or measurement contexts.
requirements: Teachers need focused time and practice on counting embedded throughout the school day, with discussion and clarification of children's ideas
constraints: The authors caution that successfully teaching advanced counting in preschool may not be sufficient for long-run impacts if kindergarten instruction does not build on it, and the underlying associations are correlational
target_learners: preschool-aged children, particularly those from low-income and minority backgrounds
target_learning_goals: early number sense, counting and cardinality, and long-run mathematics achievement
examples: The study coded REMA items into basic counting (verbal counting, one-to-one correspondence, number recognition) and advanced counting (cardinality, counting forward or back from a given number, conceptual subitizing) and found advanced counting more predictive

article_title: Conversations with AutoTutor Help Students Learn
citation: Graesser, A. C. (2016). Conversations with AutoTutor Help Students Learn. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0086-4
title: Expectation & misconception-tailored (EMT) dialogue as the core conversation mechanism of AutoTutor and human tutoring
description: EMT dialogue is a conversation mechanism in which the tutor anticipates particular correct answers (expectations) and particular misunderstandings (misconceptions) when asking challenging questions, then tracks student answers across multiple conversational turns via semantic pattern matching. The tutor gives short positive, neutral, or negative feedback and uses pumps ("What else"), hints, or prompts to elicit expectations, contributing assertions when the student fails. The pump-hint-prompt-assertion cycles are implemented in AutoTutor and are frequent in human tutoring. EMT is computationally feasible because it relies on pattern completion rather than interpreting natural language from scratch.
requirements: Requires anticipating the expectations and misconceptions for each question in advance and a semantic matching mechanism to compare student contributions against them
constraints: Relies on semantic pattern matching because full natural language interpretation is beyond reliable NLP boundaries
target_learning_goals: deep conceptual answers to challenging questions and problems in domains such as physics and research methods
examples: The mechanism was documented from near 100 videotaped, transcribed tutoring sessions with middle school children in mathematics and college students in research methods, then implemented in AutoTutor.

article_title: The Effect of Authority on the Persuasiveness of Mathematical Arguments
citation: Matthew Inglis, Juan Pablo Mejia-Ramos. (2008). The Effect of Authority on the Persuasiveness of Mathematical Arguments.
title: Empower students by reducing their uncertainty about arguments rather than suppressing appeals to authority
description: Because the studies show that reliance on authority appears mainly when readers are uncertain about an argument's status, the authors argue that "relying upon, or looking for, an authority figure should not be seen as undesirable behavior per se." Instead, instruction should focus on "empowering students by ensuring that they are in a position where they do not need to take into account an authority figure", i.e. where they have little uncertainty about the mathematical status of formal arguments. This reframes existing pedagogy that explicitly discourages appeals to expert opinion.
requirements: Instruction must give students enough mathematical resources that they experience little uncertainty about the arguments they evaluate
constraints: The authors note greater mathematical maturity is not always correlated with less uncertainty, as the visual-argument case shows researchers were more uncertain than students
target_learning_goals: evaluating mathematical arguments independently of source cues
developing mathematical reasoning about proofs
examples: The article contrasts this approach with instruction designed by Cobb & Yackel, Harel & Sowder, and Stylianides that explicitly discourages students from taking authority into account

description: A model synthesizing significant LSA transitions and mined subsequences across the four classes into five primary paths of emotional evolution: Path 1 joyful engagement with resolvable confusion (joy–curiosity–confusion–joy), Path 2 unresolved confusion leading to boredom (joy–curiosity–confusion–boredom), Path 3 extending to frustration–surprise–anxiety, Path 4 returning from anxiety to joy (joy–curiosity–confusion–boredom–frustration–surprise-anxiety-joy), and Path 5 curiosity-boredom. citation: Jan van der Meij, Marije van Amelsvoort, Anjo Anjewierden. (2017). How design guides learning from matrix diagrams. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9425-1
title: Eye Movement Sequence (EMS) model for identifying reading sequences from fixations
description: The EMS model is an algorithm the authors developed for an earlier study to identify reading sequences from eye-tracking fixation data over look zones. It scores a sequence after each fixation, updating with the maximum of the current score and fixation duration when the next fixation is compatible, and subtracting a constant times the fixation duration when it deviates; if the score becomes negative the sequence terminates. In this study a constant C of 2.0 was used, meaning an out-of-sequence fixation could be at most half the longest in-sequence fixation, and minimally three subsequent row or column look zones had to be present to count as a sequence.
requirements: Fixation data segmented into look zones (here 24, one per header and body cell), with a minimum of three subsequent row or column look zones to count as a sequence
constraints: The constant C was experimentally validated and set to 2.0 in this study; sequences terminate when the score becomes negative
target_learning_goals: reading order and processing of matrix diagrams
examples: The model classified sequences such as [5, 6, 7, 8] as strict left-to-right sequences and tolerated temporary deviations like looking at a header cell to integrate information

citation: Ilana Seidel Horn, Yeliz Günal Aggül, Shuqin Li, Christine E. Hood. (2025). Teachers’ subjectivities in responsive instruction: when ambitious practice encounters challenging teaching situations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09742-7
title: Emotional rules of responsive teaching and the surface-acting/deep-acting account of teachers' emotional labor
description: The article argues that responsive instruction carries its own emotional rules — teachers should be welcoming, present, and attuned to students — and that meeting them requires emotional labor, the work of managing internal emotions to fit situational rules. When internal feelings misalign with these rules, teachers manage the conflict through surface acting, superficially abiding while feeling discomfort, or deep acting, where teachers "actively change their attention to and interpretations of whatever is unsettling them." Deep acting reflects epistemic agency and depends on relational agency and a supportive environment offering knowledge, psychological resources, and professional discretion.
requirements: A supportive environment offering teachers knowledge, psychological resources, and latitude for professional discretion for deep acting
constraints: Hochschild's emotional labor construct presumes a stable authentic self, which the authors replace with dynamic, negotiated subjectivities
target_learning_goals: managing the emotional labor of maintaining empathetic, inclusive classroom environments
examples: Veronica's surface acting: swallowing fear and anxiety around Luca while presenting a pleasant demeanor; Linda's shift to deep acting after entertaining the possibility Bee was neurodivergent

title: Three complementary theoretical perspectives on why EMME foster multimedia learning (attentional, metacognitive, social-cognitive)
description: The article organizes explanations of EMME effectiveness into three perspectives that are "not mutually exclusive, but are likely to complement each other". From an attentional perspective, EMME highlight relevant information like other attention-guiding cues and may trigger synchronization processes establishing joint attention. From a (meta-)cognitive perspective, observing the model's gaze is assumed to support acquiring or regulating cognitive processing strategies, treating EMME as a particular type of video modeling example. From a social-cognitive perspective, EMME induce a social learning situation whose salience, per social agency theory, leads learners to process material more deeply.
requirements: For the social perspective to apply, learners must be able to interpret the abstract gaze cue as human gaze behavior, which the authors argue is enabled by informing learners of the cue's human origin in the introductory text.
constraints: The article states these perspectives are theoretical assumptions about mechanisms, not mutually exclusive tested alternatives.

Deeper processing via perceived social interaction
examples: The article cites Chisari et al. (2020) showing learners with EMME-guidance looked faster at referenced information, and Grant and Spivey (2003) on attention direction improving reasoning, as supporting the attentional perspective.

description: The article recommends integrating three worked-example strategies into textbook practice problems: "self-explanation prompts, incorrect examples, and fading out worked examples". Correct worked examples with self-explanation prompts reduce cognitive demands and focus processing on structural features; incorrect examples force students to confront misconceptions; fading provides an appropriate challenge as knowledge builds. In the study, 22 of the 70 core practice problems in the probability unit were replaced with these example types while lesson segments stayed identical.
requirements: Worked examples should be embedded in the existing curriculum's practice segments so treatment and control students work the same problems
Incorrect examples should be highlighted as incorrect or paired with self-explanation prompts to avoid object instantiation of wrongful solutions
Fading works best when the last solution steps are omitted
constraints: The benefit dissipates for learners with higher domain knowledge (expertise reversal effect), so fading is needed as knowledge builds
target_learning_goals: probabilistic reasoning
proportional reasoning
examples: In the study, 22 of the 70 core practice problems in the What Do You Expect? probability unit were replaced with correct worked examples (7 items), partially completed worked examples (10 items), and incorrect worked examples (5 items), with 14 self-explanation items total
key_sources: Begolli, K. N., Dai, T., McGinn, K. M., & Booth, J. L. (2021). Could probability be out of proportion? Self-explanation and example-based practice help students with lower proportional reasoning skills learn probability. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09550-9

article_title: Ten steps to 4C/ID: training differentiation skills in a professional development program for teachers
citation: Frerejean, J., van Geel, M., Keuning, T., Dolmans, D., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Visscher, A. J. (2021). Ten steps to 4C/ID: training differentiation skills in a professional development program for teachers. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09540-x
title: Emphasis manipulation: sequencing workplace learning tasks by shifting attentional focus across skill clusters
description: When learners practice in authentic workplace settings, designers cannot control task complexity or sequence, so simple-to-complex task classes are impossible. 4C/ID's alternative keeps tasks at natural complexity while actively allocating learner attention to one aspect or skill cluster at a time. The article explains that "4C/ID offers an alternative emphasis manipulation approach, in which learners carry out learning tasks (i.e., their daily mathematics lessons) in their natural complexity, but attention is actively allocated to just an aspect of the task or a certain skill cluster." The PD program used this across four task classes, moving the spotlight from lesson introductions and endings to monitoring, adapting instruction, and finally self-regulation.
requirements: All activities, supportive materials, and coaching must be directed at the emphasized aspect; a logical order of aspects must be determined
constraints: Errors may be expected in aspects not yet emphasized, leading to suboptimal task performance; the approach reduces but does not eliminate the need for load management
target_learners: in-service teachers learning during daily classroom practice
target_learning_goals: managing cognitive load while acquiring a complex professional skill in the workplace
examples: Task classes emphasized lesson introductions/endings, then monitoring, then monitoring plus adapting instruction, then stimulating self-regulation

article_title: Online teaching in networked learning communities: A multi-method approach to studying the role of the teacher
citation: de Laat, M., Lally, V., Lipponen, L. & Simons, R.-J. (2007). Online teaching in networked learning communities: A multi-method approach to studying the role of the teacher. Instructional Science, vol. 35, no. 3, pp. 257-286. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-006-9007-0
title: Experienced online tutor's facilitation pattern: emergent group learning with subtle peripheral scaffolding
description: The experienced tutor's pattern is to let the group be emergent, letting participants seek their own rhythms and ways of working, while staying present peripherally and building a subtle support framework the group can use as it progresses. He reported: "My teaching style is to let the group be emergent in their learning and let them seek their own rhythms and ways of working and learning together." He used advanced organisers to pre-organise process and project issues, sounded notes of caution to keep the project do-able, and drew on a mental framework of pitfalls to create scaffolding he could pull back when necessary.
requirements: trust and sensitivity on the part of the teacher not to interfere immediately with learner activities
a general understanding and pedagogical framework of the course built from prior experience
constraints: the group did not take up the process organiser when offered early, being interested only in content at that stage
target_learners: mid-career professionals in online networked learning communities
target_learning_goals: collaborative course design for online learning
self- and group-regulation of learning
examples: The tutor put in an advanced organiser with two headings, one to organise the process and one to identify a project, and built an architectural framework through his messages that participants could realise themselves

article_title: Teachers rehumanizing mathematics for students with disabilities; the role of empathy
citation: Rachel Lambert, Kara Imm. (2026). Teachers rehumanizing mathematics for students with disabilities; the role of empathy. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09753-4
title: A model integrating empathy with teacher knowledge as politically situated and emergent in relationship with marginalized students
description: Building on the new uses educators made of empathy, the authors propose a model that integrates empathy with conceptualizations of teachers' knowledge as "both politically situated and emergent in relationship with marginalized students." The model links design thinking, with empathy as its central value and practice, to surrounding knowledges: political conocimiento, models of disability, UDL Math, and political knowledge for teaching mathematics to students with disability. It treats teacher knowledge as relational, emotional, and unfolding over time rather than static.
requirements: Educators engage in empathy as both a value and a repeated practice (empathy interviews) in relationship with students
constraints: The model was developed from one professional-development study conducted during the 2020–2021 pandemic year of primarily remote teaching
target_learners: Mathematics teachers and special educators of students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Rehumanizing mathematics instruction; shifting away from deficit views of disability
examples: Participants came to see empathy as the unifying concept between rethinking deficit assumptions about students and noticing and challenging unjust systems in special education and mathematics.
