article_title: Enhancing learning of nanoscale phenomena: the role of agent-based models and embodied reasoning
citation: Polly K. Lai. (2026). Enhancing learning of nanoscale phenomena: the role of agent-based models and embodied reasoning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09776-x
title: Embodied cognition framework of three embodied processes—perspective taking, causal inference making, and motor-supported thinking—for learning with ABMs
description: The article operationalizes embodied cognition (drawing on Clark's account of emergent patterns and Barsalou's grounded cognition) as three indicators of learning with ABMs. "These three indicators—perspective taking, causal inference making, and motor-supported thinking—operationalize how embodied cognition is enacted differently in ABMs versus visualisations and provided a coding framework for this study." Perspective taking involves shifting between agent-level (first-person) and system-level (third-person) viewpoints; causal inference making links parameter changes to system outcomes through manipulation; motor-supported thinking uses gestures and handwriting to externalise mental simulations. The framework guided both the intervention design and the reasoning-strategy coding scheme.
requirements: Learning environments must afford manipulation of agents or parameters so learners can shift perspectives, test causal inferences, and gesture; visualizations that only present pre-structured animations limit embodied exploration
constraints: The framework was developed and tested for nanoscience concepts (size-dependent properties, surface-area-to-volume ratio) with undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: explanatory understanding of emergent nanoscale phenomena
applying size-dependent properties concepts to novel problems
examples: The study coded post-test think-aloud protocols and bodily movements using the three indicators, adapted from Chi's (1997) method, achieving Kappa κ =.86
key_sources: Polly K. Lai. (2026). Enhancing learning of nanoscale phenomena: the role of agent-based models and embodied reasoning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09776-x

article_title: Examining metacognitive strategy use in L1 and L2 task-situated writing: effects, transferability, and cross-language facilitation
citation: Wandong Xu, Xinhua Zhu. (2024). Examining metacognitive strategy use in L1 and L2 task-situated writing: effects, transferability, and cross-language facilitation. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09387-w
title: Embed metacognitive strategy training in writing classrooms with explicit, practical guidance across task interpreting, planning, monitoring, and evaluating
description: The article recommends training metacognitive strategies as a pedagogical tool in writing classrooms, given their predictive effects on L1 and L2 writing performance and the malleability of metacognition. It specifies that "explicit guidance is needed to help students form an accurate task representation, generate logical pre-plans, execute effective monitoring linguistically and non-linguistically, and have meaningful evaluations", and that "Practical guidance appears to be more effective than vague explanations".
requirements: Training should be embedded in the writing classroom as learners sit in writing tasks and writing-related activities instead of being decontextualized
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive regulation of the writing process
L1 and L2 writing performance
examples: The study's five validated strategy subcategories (task interpreting, planning, non-linguistic monitoring, linguistic monitoring, evaluating) structure the recommended training content

article_title: Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation
citation: Wirth, J., Weber-Reuter, X.-L., Schuster, C., Fleischer, J., Leutner, D., & Stebner, F. (2025). Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09983-x
title: Effort Monitoring and Regulation (EMR) framework for metacognitive regulation of investing mental effort
description: The article describes the EMR framework, proposed by de Bruin et al. (2020) and building on Nelson and Narens' (1990) model, as one that "describe[s] the processes of metacognitive regulation of investing mental effort." Monitoring relies on perceiving and interpreting cues (e.g., perceived demand characteristics, speed and fluency of performance) to form effort appraisals of both required and invested mental effort; because learners cannot directly evaluate learning at the object level, they infer from cues and may use invalid cues or misinterpret them. Control can be data-driven (experienced required effort triggers more invested effort) or goal-driven (learners instead adapt goals, reducing required effort). The article applies EMR to define goal-setting, planning, monitoring, and controlling specifically for mental effort regulation.
requirements: Learners need good metacognitive knowledge to decide which cues to look for, which the article says results from previous experience with the task type and reflection on it
constraints: Cue perception and interpretation are easier for familiar than unfamiliar learning tasks; the meta-level model may represent the object level imperfectly, so subjective and actual effort can diverge
target_learners: school students (5th and 6th grade in the study)
target_learning_goals: metacognitive regulation of investing mental effort during learning tasks
examples: The study operationalized EMR-style regulation as an effort regulation score subtracting required from invested mental effort ratings after each task

article_title: Attention and Long-Term Memory in System and Process Theories of Working Memory: A Reply to Soemer’s (2015) Comment on Schweppe and Rummer (2014)
citation: Judith Schweppe & Ralf Rummer. (2015). Attention and Long-Term Memory in System and Process Theories of Working Memory: A Reply to Soemer's (2015) Comment on Schweppe and Rummer (2014). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9336-0
title: The embedded-processes model as a unitary framework for attention, working memory, and long-term memory in multimedia learning
description: The article advocates Cowan's (1999) embedded-processes model as the working-memory framework for multimedia learning theory. Unlike the multicomponent model, it conceives of working memory as the interplay of attentional processes and long-term memory, allowing multimedia principles to be explained in a unitary manner. The authors state it "provides an integrated account of the cognitive processes that are most relevant for learning with text and pictures (attention and long-term memory) and their interaction."
requirements: A framework must already provide a unified account of attention, working memory, and long-term memory to serve multimedia learning theory
constraints: The authors do not claim the multicomponent model should be rejected; they argue the embedded-processes model is the more productive focus for multimedia research
target_learners: learners with multimedia learning materials (text and pictures)
target_learning_goals: explaining cognitive constraints on learning with text and pictures

article_title: Effects of Rubrics on Academic Performance, Self-Regulated Learning, and self-Efficacy: a Meta-analytic Review
citation: Panadero, Ernesto; Jonsson, Anders; Pinedo, Leire; Fernández-Castilla, Belén. (2023). Effects of Rubrics on Academic Performance, Self-Regulated Learning, and self-Efficacy: a Meta-analytic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09823-4
title: Empirical-quality rubric instrument for evaluating rubric studies
description: The authors designed an instrument to rate the empirical quality of rubric intervention studies, consisting of "a rubric with the following categories: research design, quality of the measurement tools, quality of the intervention (three subcategories: training, practice, length of the intervention), quality of dependent variables, and quality of the sample." Each study was scored on all categories to compute a summary quality score, used as a moderator. They also provide it "to be filled out for rubric scholars in forthcoming studies" to improve reporting quality. Data and coding are shared via an OSF link printed in the article.
requirements: Studies must be codable on research design, measurement tools, intervention quality, dependent variables, and sample quality
target_learning_goals: improving quality and reporting of rubric intervention research
examples: Applied to the 24 included studies to compute an empirical quality score used in moderator analyses
key_sources: Panadero, Ernesto; Jonsson, Anders; Pinedo, Leire; Fernández-Castilla, Belén. (2023). Effects of Rubrics on Academic Performance, Self-Regulated Learning, and self-Efficacy: a Meta-analytic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09823-4

article_title: The Cronbach’s Alpha of Domain-Specific Knowledge Tests Before and After Learning: A Meta-Analysis of Published Studies
citation: Peter A. Edelsbrunner, Bianca A. Simonsmeier, Michael Schneider. (2025). The Cronbach’s Alpha of Domain‑Specific Knowledge Tests Before and After Learning: A Meta‑Analysis of Published Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09982-y
title: Judge knowledge test internal consistency against empirically based expectations rather than fixed Alpha cut-offs
description: The article argues that fixed cut-off values (e.g., 0.70) for knowledge test Alphas lack theoretical or empirical basis and bias research by suppressing publication of heterogeneous knowledge tests. Instead, researchers should compare their test's Alpha against empirically derived prediction intervals that account for test length. The authors note "dropping guidelines altogether may be a better way forward."
requirements: Researchers need the expected Alpha range for their test length, derivable from the Spearman–Brown prophecy formula applied to the meta-analytic estimate.
constraints: The proposed prediction interval guideline applies to knowledge tests with about 20 items; the article provides separate guidelines for shorter and longer tests.
target_learners: Educational researchers developing and evaluating domain-specific knowledge tests
target_learning_goals: Valid measurement of domain-specific knowledge before and after learning
examples: The meta-analysis derived a 90% prediction interval of [0.35, 0.96] as a guideline for Alphas of knowledge tests with 20 items, with guidelines for shorter and longer tests.

article_title: Building Bridges Between Self-Regulation and Cognitive Load—an Invitation for a Broad and Differentiated Attempt
citation: Tina Seufert. (2020). Building Bridges Between Self-Regulation and Cognitive Load—an Invitation for a Broad and Differentiated Attempt. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 1151–1162. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09574-6
title: Effort Monitoring and Regulation (EMR) framework linking self-regulated learning with mental effort and cognitive load
description: The EMR-framework, introduced by the special-issue editors (de Bruin, Roelle, Baars, and the EARLI Emerging Field Group), builds a bridge from self-regulation to cognitive load by linking self-regulated learning with mental effort. The review states that "mental effort is crucial for dealing with the task as well as for self-regulation," and that awareness of invested resources "can serve as a cue to inform processes both on the object-level and on the meta-level." At its center is the CLT differentiation of intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load, though most papers measure effort with a one-item rating. The framework frames all nine papers, which stimulate learning on the object level, for effort utilization, or on the meta-level.
requirements: Learners must be aware of their invested resources so these can serve as cues for monitoring and regulation
constraints: Effort appraisals in the framed papers are mostly measured with a one-item rating and are not differentiated into intrinsic, extraneous, and germane categories
target_learners: Learners in self-regulated learning settings, including learners studying on their own
target_learning_goals: Improved monitoring accuracy and regulation of learning through use of effort cues
examples: The special-issue papers apply the framework via generative tasks, effort-utilization training, and meta-level journal writing

article_title: Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review
citation: Carolien Duijzer, Marja Van den Heuvel-Panhuizen, Michiel Veldhuis, Michiel Doorman, & Paul Leseman. (2019). Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09471-7
title: Two-dimensional taxonomy of embodied learning environments for graphing motion based on bodily involvement and immediacy
description: The review proposes categorizing embodied learning environments for graphing motion on two dimensions: bodily involvement (own motion vs. observing/influencing others' or objects' motion, ranging from "motor execution" to "motor mirroring") and immediacy (immediate vs. non-immediate, from "direct enactment" to "reactivated enactment"). Crossing these dimensions yields four classes: Class I — Immediate Own Motion, Class II — Immediate Others/Objects' Motion, Class III — Non-immediate Own Motion, and Class IV — Non-immediate Others/Objects' Motion. The authors state: "we propose to categorize embodied learning environments supporting students ' understanding of graphing motion on two dimensions: bodily involvement and immediacy". Immediacy concerns whether the graphical representation is constructed in parallel with the motion or at a later stage.
requirements: Learning environments must contain task-relevant bodily experiences that can be coded on bodily involvement and immediacy; environments with multiple degrees are assigned to the highest degree
constraints: The authors note task integration is a less informative dimension for graphing motion because "the congruency between a motion event (either experienced or observed) and the graph of that motion is already an essential element of the learning environment"
target_learners: Students from primary education to higher education in mathematics and physics
target_learning_goals: Understanding graphical representations of motion (distance–time, velocity–time, acceleration–time graphs)
examples: The 62 reviewed learning environments were classified into the four classes; Class I contained 34 environments, Class II and IV 12 each, and Class III 4
key_sources: Carolien Duijzer, Marja Van den Heuvel-Panhuizen, Michiel Veldhuis, Michiel Doorman, & Paul Leseman. (2019). Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09471-7

article_title: Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review
citation: Carolien Duijzer, Marja Van den Heuvel-Panhuizen, Michiel Veldhuis, Michiel Doorman, & Paul Leseman. (2019). Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09471-7
title: Review corpus of 44 peer-reviewed articles comprising 62 embodied learning environments for graphing motion
description: The review's evidence base is a corpus of 44 empirical, peer-reviewed journal articles in English, identified through searches in Web of Science, ERIC, PsycINFO, and Scopus (initial 1953 articles, 1651 after deduplication) plus snowballing. "The 44 articles contained a total of 62 different embodied learning environments", some used as control and some as experimental conditions. Each environment was coded on bodily involvement and immediacy; an independent second rater coded a subsample of 12 articles containing 20 learning environments, with Cohen's Kappa = 1.00 for bodily involvement and 0.74 for immediacy. All articles addressed mathematics, physics, or both, with graphs representing motion data.
requirements: Included articles needed a clear description of tools and tasks and task-relevant bodily experiences
constraints: The number of bodily actions and their duration was not coded due to lacking information in most articles
target_learners: Students from primary education to higher education
target_learning_goals: Learning graphing of change and motion in mathematics and physics
examples: The search flowchart reports 1953 initial articles reduced to 36 relevant articles, with 13 added by snowballing and 5 excluded for lacking description of the embodied learning environment

citation: Theobald, M., Kerner auch Koerner, J., Breitwieser, J., Buhr, L., Karbach, J., Könönen, T., Nobbe, L., Reinelt, T., Schaaf, M., Schmiedek, F., Wieland, L. M., & Blume, F. (2026). Executive Functions, Metacognition, Self-Regulation, and Self-Regulated Learning – What are We Talking About? A Review and Introduction of the EMERGE Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10157-0
title: The EMERGE model positions EF, MC, SR and SRL along a continuum from biologically grounded mechanics to culturally shaped pragmatics
description: The EMERGE model is a conceptual framework introduced by this review to integrate four research traditions that have been examined in isolation. It positions EF, MC, SR and SRL along a continuum, "ranging from more biologically grounded mechanics (e.g., EF) to more culturally shaped pragmatics (e.g., strategy knowledge in SRL)", and conceptualises SR in learning situations as an integrative construct. The model highlights both shared mechanisms and distinct functions of the four constructs in learning processes.
requirements: The model is intended to bridge fragmented research traditions that have examined EF, MC, SR and SRL in isolation due to disciplinary and methodological divides
constraints: The review's focus is on school-aged children, as the four constructs demonstrate significant development during this stage of life

goal-directed learning behaviour

article_title: Embodied learning and teaching approaches in language education: A mixed studies review
citation: Sofia Jusslin, Kaisa Korpinen, Niina Lilja, Rose Martin, Johanna Lehtinen-Schnabel, Eeva Anttila. (2022). Embodied learning and teaching approaches in language education: A mixed studies review. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2022.100480
title: Embodied learning as holistic engagement: bodily engagement beyond motor action, grounded in 4E cognition
description: The review defines embodied learning as "a conception of learning where learners are holistically engaged and intertwined in their social and material surroundings", rooted in the embodied turn and phenomenology. Drawing on Barsalou's grounded/4E cognition account, it argues embodied activity goes beyond visible movement to include inner bodily sensations and physiological changes, and proposes that "embodied learning extends beyond learning through movement and that a more suitable term for learning through motor action could be bodily learning". This framework underpins the review's analysis and its openness to multiple theoretical perspectives.
requirements: Understanding cognition as embodied connecting brain, body, and environment, rather than a modular brain-bound view
constraints: The review contests the claim that all learning is embodied simply because the brain is part of the body, requiring more detailed argumentation
target_learners: language learners from early childhood to adulthood
target_learning_goals: language learning and teaching understood as an embodied process
examples: The review distinguishes embodied learning from kinesthetic learning, which it describes as pedagogical practices emphasizing sensory (kinesthetic) experiences generated through bodily activity

article_title: What If We Look at the Body? An Embodied Perspective of Collaborative Learning
citation: Juliene Madureira Ferreira. (2021). What If We Look at the Body? An Embodied Perspective of Collaborative Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09607-8
title: Embodied cognition theory as a framework for investigating collaborative learning
description: The review proposes embodied cognition (EC) as a theoretical lens for collaborative learning, holding that 'the only way that the brain talks to the environment is through the body, sensory tissues, and organs.' EC spans moderate approaches based on bodily formats and embodied simulation, radical enactive approaches where perception directly picks up others' mental states, and extended cognition where the cognitive loop encompasses brain, body, and environment. The article argues this lens can reveal how collaboration skills emerge through bodily engagements and intersubjectivity, dimensions regulatory-systems frameworks cannot reach.
requirements: Researchers must acknowledge the brain as embodied, treating sensorimotor experiences as a fundamental unit of analysis in investigating cognitive processes including knowledge construction.
constraints: The article states EC theories do not refute the validity of traditional cognitivist approaches but provide an alternative explanation for how human knowledge is constructed.
target_learners: students in group-based learning from early childhood to higher education
target_learning_goals: collaboration as a transversal competence
knowledge construction in groups
examples: The review applies EC to propose analyzing bodily engagements, nonverbal behaviors, physiological synchrony, and intersubjectivity during face-to-face collaborative tasks.

article_title: Emotions Are Not Random: Machine Learning Reveals Predictable Patterns in a 21-Day Second Language Learning Trajectory
citation: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2026). Emotions Are Not Random: Machine Learning Reveals Predictable Patterns in a 21-Day Second Language Learning Trajectory. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10141-8
title: 21-day EMA dataset of 6,918 language-learning episodes with momentary emotions, perceived proficiency and contextual features
description: An intensive longitudinal dataset in which 92 adult foreign language learners completed momentary surveys via the Avicenna app (four per day at 2-hour intervals plus one end-of-day survey) over 21 days, yielding "6,918 momentary surveys (EMA prompts)". Each survey captured single-item ratings of anxiety, enjoyment, boredom and perceived proficiency (0–10 scales) plus contextual features: modality, activity type (self-directed vs. classroom), episode duration, time since the last activity and time until the next. Overall response rate was 71.4% with median per-person compliance of 83.3%.
requirements: Smartphone-based EMA prompting with one-hour response windows to minimize recall bias, and single-item indicators justified by dense sampling
constraints: Compliance ranged from 1.9% to 100% across participants; most learning was self-directed (85.0%) and speaking and writing episodes were relatively rare
target_learners: adult foreign language learners (Chinese university students, mean age 20.1)
target_learning_goals: tracking momentary emotions and self-perceived proficiency during self-directed and classroom language learning
examples: 41.5% of episodes mixed at least two modalities; mean episode length was 40.9 minutes.

citation: Alexander Skulmowski. (2024). Learning by Doing or Doing Without Learning? The Potentials and Challenges of Activity-Based Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09869-y
title: Taxonomies of embodied learning classifying interventions by bodily engagement, task integration, and relevance
description: The review organizes movement-based learning research through successive classification systems. Johnson-Glenberg et al. (2014) proposed three factors: motoric engagement, gestural congruency, and immersion. Skulmowski and Rey (2018) simplified this to "the two dimensions bodily engagement and task integration," finding bodily engagement has a nonlinear influence on learning. Mavilidi et al. (2022) proposed a 2x2 system with the dimensions integration (temporal connection between movements and tasks) and relevance (correspondence between movements and content). These taxonomies predict when motor activity helps or hinders learning.

constraints: Skulmowski and Rey (2018) describe excessive bodily activity as linked to extraneous cognitive load, so more engagement is not always better
target_learners: learners in embodied and movement-based learning interventions
target_learning_goals: selecting and designing motor activities that support rather than distract from learning
examples: The review uses the taxonomies to explain why whole-body movement studies do not always outperform less bodily activity

title: Three mechanisms underlying EMME effectiveness: attention guidance, revealing perceptual strategies, and inducing a social learning situation
description: The review adopts Krebs et al.'s account that EMME effectiveness rests on three mechanisms. Gaze visualizations act as "visual cue to guide the observer's attention", helping observers select relevant information at the right time in transient instructional videos; they reveal "a performer's perceptual strategies that would otherwise not be accessible to observers", since people have limited insight into their own viewing behavior; and they induce a stronger social learning situation, evoking more social presence than abstract cues such as animated arrows. The review coded which of these rationales each included study used.
requirements: Gaze visualization must be displayed on top of to-be-learned task material with the goal of fostering observer performance or learning
constraints: The review treats these as rationales stated by study authors, not as mechanisms tested within this review

acquisition of expert perceptual and cognitive strategies

title: Embodied-design instructional sequence: motor challenge, emergent attentional anchor, quantitative re-articulation, then formal mathematical discourse

constraints: Documented in cross-sectional qualitative studies; the article notes studies have been cross-sectional rather than longitudinal

The commentary states it details "a single central executive (i.e., attentional) mechanism that is able to (re)activate any long-term memory trace irrespective of its content". Cowan argued for this general mechanism based on experiments showing working memory capacity estimates do not differ much between single and dual span tasks with verbal and visual materials under certain conditions. The commentary treats this model as complementary to, not a replacement for, the multicomponent model.

constraints: The commentary notes functional specialization is "not paid attention to in the embedded-processes model"

citation: Anique B. H. de Bruin, Felicitas Biwer, Luotong Hui, Erdem Onan, Louise David, Wisnu Wiradhany. (2023). Worth the Effort: the Start and Stick to Desirable Difficulties (S2D2) Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09766-w

description: The EMR model, on which S2D2 builds, describes how cycles of monitoring and regulation of learning characterize learning task engagement, extending the Nelson and Narens metalevel/object-level architecture. Monitoring results are brought to the metalevel, and control is exerted to translate decisions back to the object level. The article states: "The EMR model outlines how effort is used as a basis for monitoring and control of learning, and how effort needs to be managed in self-regulated learning environments." S2D2 focuses on the model's first two research questions, how students monitor and regulate effort.

constraints: S2D2 addresses only the first two EMR research questions (monitoring and regulating effort)

description: The EMR model "integrates self-regulated learning and cognitive load theory to examine how students monitor, regulate, and optimize effort during learning." Introduced in 2020 by an EARLI and Jacobs Foundation-sponsored Emerging Field Group, it poses three research questions: how students monitor effort, how they regulate effort, and how cognitive load on SRL tasks can be optimized during and after the primary task. The topical collection papers are mapped onto the model and used to refine it.

constraints: The editorial notes critical questions remain, including how learners transition from data-driven to goal-driven interpretations of effort

citation: Scott C. Marley & Kira J. Carbonneau. (2014). Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives: Commentary on the Special Issue Papers. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9259-1
title: Embedded and embodied cognition account: perceptually rich, interactive manipulatives may improve transfer through internalization of multimodality routines
description: Pouw, van Gog, and Paas's account, discussed in the commentary, draws on embedded and embodied cognitive viewpoints to propose that learning with manipulatives is "a complex interplay between structuring and restructuring the environment (i.e., embedded cognition) and a cognitive system consisting of manipulations of perceptual symbols (i.e., embodied cognition)". constraints: Convincing evidence supporting this and related predictions is currently scarce, as the commentary notes

citation: Björn B. de Koning, Lisanne T. Bos, Stephanie I. Wassenburg & Menno van der Schoot. (2017). Effects of a Reading Strategy Training Aimed at Improving Mental Simulation in Primary School Children. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 869–889. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9380-4
title: Embodied situation model account of reading comprehension via mental simulation
description: The article frames reading comprehension as constructing a situation model whose representations are partially based on reactivations of the brain areas governing analogous perception and action. It states that "understanding text involves a mental simulation of described events by reactivating and integrating traces of earlier experiences from multiple perceptual and motor modalities in the brain". Readers who simulate perceptual and motoric elements build an embodied situation model assumed to yield deeper understanding; the training tested whether this process can be taught.
requirements: Readers must retrieve and integrate their stored sensorimotor experiences with the events and objects mentioned in the text
constraints: The article notes mental simulation is a multifaceted concept of which the administered tasks capture only a specific aspect
target_learners: primary school children in Grades 3 and 4
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension via construction of an embodied situation model
examples: The training taught children to use all their senses to represent described events, to simulate implicitly described object shapes, and to simulate implied movement directions

citation: Björn B. de Koning & Huib K. Tabbers. (2011). Facilitating Understanding of Movements in Dynamic Visualizations: an Embodied Perspective. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9173-8
title: Embodied cognition: cognition grounded in perception and action via multimodal simulations
description: The article adopts embodied theories of cognition, in which psychological processes are shaped by the body and its interaction with the world, as the theoretical framework for improving learning from animations. Central to the account are simulations, defined as "the reenactment of perceptual and motor states that were acquired during experiences with the physical world"; even abstract concepts are understood by mapping concrete, bodily grounded concepts onto them. The article uses this framework to argue that sensorimotor experiences during learning become part of the mental simulation and enrich learners' multimodal representations of depicted movements.
requirements: Learning content must be linkable to learners' perceptual and motor experiences for embodiment to support representation building
constraints: The article notes the mirror neuron variant of this account remains speculative because the exact mechanisms translating neural activation into learning benefits have yet to be identified
target_learners: learners studying mechanical or technical processes via dynamic visualizations
target_learning_goals: building accurate mental representations of the movements of dynamic systems
examples: The article interprets action–sentence compatibility effects and motor cortex activation during language comprehension as evidence that comprehension entails mental simulation of described actions

citation: de Bruin, A. B. H., Roelle, J., Carpenter, S. K., & Baars, M. (2020). Synthesizing Cognitive Load and Self-regulation Theory: a Theoretical Framework and Research Agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09576-4
title: The Effort Monitoring and Regulation (EMR) framework integrates cognitive load theory with self-regulated learning theory
description: The EMR framework builds on the Nelson and Narens model, positing a meta level at which metacognitive monitoring and regulation occur based on input from the object level where learners engage with a learning task. Cognitive load is positioned in the middle, with direct links to both levels and both processes. The authors state it "outlines how monitoring and regulation of effort are neglected but essential aspects of self-regulated learning" and emphasize optimizing cognitive load during self-regulated learning by reducing unnecessary primary-task load or distributing load between the primary task and metacognitive aspects.

constraints: Beyond effort cues, various other cues (e.g., fluency, familiarity) affect monitoring, regulation, and learning
Interactions with individual differences, task characteristics, and learning context need to be taken into account
Integrated CLT-SRL research is in its embryonal stage, with little empirical data to date

target_learning_goals: accurate self-monitoring of learning and effort

citation: Janssen, E. M., van Gog, T., van de Groep, L., de Lange, A. J., Knopper, R. L., Onan, E., Wiradhany, W., & de Bruin, A. B. H. (2023). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09797-3
title: Effort Monitoring and Regulation (EMR) framework
description: The EMR framework, attributed by the article to De Bruin et al. (2020), "proposes that students use mental effort as a cue for monitoring their learning and for making study decisions." It explains why students avoid effective but effortful strategies: they may misinterpret experienced effort during studying, treating the experience that studying costs much effort as an indication that they are not learning well. The present experiments tested this account by relating effort ratings to judgments of learning, perceived strategy effectiveness, and willingness to use blocked and interleaved study.

constraints: The article applies the framework to conditions, like interleaved studying, where high effort investment may actually result in higher learning outcomes

examples: Both experiments measured self-reported mental effort, judgments of learning, perceived effectiveness, and willingness to use each strategy at multiple measurement moments

citation: de Koning, B., Zhang, S., & Sepp, S. (2025). Integrating Human Movement in Learning: Advancements in Language Instruction, Multimedia, and Theory. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10027-1
title: Embodied cognition with biologically primary movement supporting biologically secondary knowledge acquisition
description: The article frames the collection with embodied cognition, the view that "cognition is situated in a real-world environment where bodies and brains are inextricably linked," so movements are not only outputs of thinking but can impact cognitive processing. Within Cognitive Load Theory, biologically primary knowledge (e.g., gesturing) is evolved, requires little cognitive effort and no explicit instruction, while biologically secondary knowledge (e.g., arithmetic) requires instruction and deliberate investment. Primary movements can support secondary knowledge acquisition, such as using hands to represent an object in space when learning the meaning of a word.
requirements: Instruction and deliberate cognitive investment are needed for biologically secondary knowledge to benefit from primary-movement support.
constraints: The framework distinguishes biologically primary from biologically secondary knowledge; the article presents it as theorizing within CLT rather than a tested result of this collection.
target_learners: learners across domains including language and mathematics
target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning
arithmetic and other instructed secondary knowledge
examples: The article cites Montessori embedding the tracing of letters on sandpaper to support children's writing more than 100 years ago.

citation: Margina Ruiter & Sofie Loyens & Fred Paas. (2015). Watch Your Step Children! Learning Two-Digit Numbers Through Mirror-Based Observation of Self-Initiated Body Movements. Educ Psychol Rev (2015) 27:457–474. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9324-4

description: The article frames its intervention with embodied cognition theories, which propose that "cognitive processes are grounded in perception and bodily action", in contrast to cognitivist approaches treating mind and body as separate. constraints: The account is the article's framing; the study's design could not determine which specific element of the movements produced the learning benefit

description: The article reformulates the Perform First Hypothesis as embodied guidance fading, an account grounded in cognitive load theory. It prescribes to "use the least embodied, task-relevant support needed for the learner's current knowledge and the task's element interactivity, then fade that support as schemas develop". The aim is better learning, transfer, and flexible use of formal representations, not movement or lower load for its own sake.

constraints: The account is formulated for embodied instruction in STEM

target_learning_goals: Concept understanding, transfer, and flexible use of formal representations
examples: Tracing a graph helps novices coordinate slope, variables, and change

article_title: Embodied guidance fading: When embodiment supports STEM learning by optimizing cognitive load
citation: Fred Paas, Nadine Marcus, Kevin Sigayret, Peng Wang, Kim Ouwehand, Liye Zou. (2026). Embodied guidance fading: When embodiment supports STEM learning by optimizing cognitive load. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2026.2717080
title: Optimize cognitive load in embodied instruction: aim for better learning and transfer, not movement or lower load for its own sake
description: This principle holds that the central instructional aim of embodied instruction is not movement or reduced load per se, but improved outcomes. The article states: "The central instructional aim is not movement or lower load for its own sake, but better learning, transfer, and flexible use of formal representations." Embodied activity should therefore be judged by whether it optimizes cognitive load toward learning, transfer, and flexible use of formal representations.
requirements: Embodied activities must be evaluated against learning, transfer, and flexible use of formal representations rather than amount of movement
target_learning_goals: Learning, transfer, and flexible use of formal representations
examples: Tracing a graph is justified when it helps novices coordinate slope, variables, and change

citation: Baier-Mosch, Franziska; Dignath, Charlotte; Kunter, Mareike (2026). Effects of heterogeneity simulations on beliefs. Learning and Instruction 101, Art. 102258. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102258
title: Empathy-and-internalization account of self-experience simulations
description: The article grounds heterogeneity simulations in experience-based learning theory drawn from disability-simulation research: simulations in which people self-experience situations of others are argued to be effective "because they lead to empathy", which comprises affective and cognitive components. Empathy is said to trigger internalization, whereby external social regulations become "internalized, personally endorsed values and beliefs". The article applies this account to explain why self-experience, but not reading a factual text, should change heterogeneity-responsive teaching beliefs.
requirements: The learner must directly experience the simulated situation (self-experience), not merely receive factual information about it
constraints: The article notes empathy was not directly measured as an explanatory mechanism in its own research
target_learning_goals: beliefs about the importance of heterogeneity-responsive teaching
examples: The heterogeneity simulation operationalized the account by having participants read simulated peer feedback revealing different perceived difficulty of the same text

article_title: Do you play in class? Board games to promote cognitive and educational development in primary school: A cluster randomized controlled trial
citation: Nuria Vita-Barrull, Verónica Estrada-Plana, Jaume March-Llanes, Pablo Sotoca-Orgaz, Núria Guzmán, Rosa Ayesa, Jorge Moya-Higueras. (2024). Do you play in class? Board games to promote cognitive and educational development in primary school: A cluster randomized controlled trial. Learning and Instruction, 93. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101946
title: Emergent and embedded learning in game-based learning
description: This framework distinguishes two ways learning arises in playful formats. "Emergent learning is understood as the acquisition of new skills and knowledge every time we face challenges that need to be overcome", whereas "embedded learning refers to learning linked to a particular context" — the inclusion of specific concepts and content in game elements, such as writing information on cards, to achieve didactic objectives. The article presents modern board games as a playful methodology that combines both: learning emerges from participation and interaction around the game while curricular content is embedded in game elements, so children playing for fun are inadvertently engaging cognitive abilities and curricular knowledge.
requirements: Games must pose challenges whose difficulty aligns with participants' capacity to sustain engagement
constraints: In these commercial games the learning content is emergent rather than explicit
target_learning_goals: executive functions
curricular academic skills
examples: In Monster Match, winning requires recognising dice numbers and counting monsters' eyes, legs, hands and doughnuts; in La Morada Maldita, higher-point cards include counting, simple arithmetic and polygon identification

article_title: Distribution of grades.
citation: J. L. Zerbe. (1917). Distribution of Grades. The Journal of Educational Psychology, VIII(10), 575-588.
title: Base grading standards on empirically derived distribution curves rather than instructors' personal opinion
description: The article argues that because instructor grading rests on personal opinion and varies wildly, institutions need "definite scales, absolute units of value for school work." It proposes that "a curve which expresses the correlation of mental tests of the students within the institution with the distribution of grades as assigned by many instructors through many years ought to give a distribution which would maintain the traditional standards of that institution and at the same time give the individual student full justice." Until a per-subject measuring scale exists, an empirically derived curve is the recommended scientific method of grading.
requirements: Either well-devised psychological tests of the students, or a multi-year distribution of grades within the institution, as the basis for the curve.
constraints: The author notes a test-based curve limits the institution's standard to the general mental ability of its students, and a curve based on former grades, while upholding tradition, "is not just in the long run to many of the students."
target_learning_goals: just, uniform recognition of school work in grades, honors, and elimination decisions
examples: Zerbe's report to the Carnegie Institute of Technology faculty tabulating 28,257 grades and testing 183 first-year students, offered as the empirical basis for such a curve.

article_title: Effects of peers’ emotions on students’ emotions, achievement goals, mental effort, and performance.
citation: Hu, Y., Elliot, A. J., Wouters, P., van der Schaaf, M., Kester, L., & Pekrun, R. (2024). Effects of peers' emotions on students' emotions, achievement goals, mental effort, and performance. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(7), 1283–1299. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000895
title: Three coexisting mechanisms of emotion transmission
description: The article frames emotion transmission — people "catching" the emotions of others — via three proposed mechanisms that "can coexist and affect the outcomes". Primitive emotional contagion holds that observers mimic facial, vocal, and postural expressions and afferent feedback triggers the same state; emotion categorization holds that categorizing an expression as an emotional state activates a similar state; social appraisal holds that appraising the situation from the expresser's expression triggers the emotion. The study uses this framework to motivate expecting transmission from peers to students in observational learning.
requirements: An expresser displaying emotional expressions (here a peer model's facial, postural, and vocal expressions in videos) that observers are exposed to
constraints: Transmission can be moderated by activity characteristics, individual differences such as the tendency to catch emotions, and social factors such as liking the expresser
target_learners: University students in observational learning of a science game
target_learning_goals: Achievement emotions during learning
Achievement goals
Mental effort and performance
examples: The article illustrates with witnessing a smile: one may mimic it, categorize it as enjoyment, or appraise that another is happy, all possibly triggering one's own enjoyment

article_title: A Significant Conference Report on Sex Education.
citation: New Publications, The Journal of Educational Psychology. (1920). https://journals.apa.org/edp/
title: Embed sex education within the whole purpose of education and of life, treating it as character education rather than a segregated special subject
description: The principle holds that sex education should not be isolated as a special subject. The 1920 conference report reviewed here argues it is "not in its nature a special form of education" but character education that addresses pervasive human incentives, and that segregation arouses apprehension. It recommends psychological gradation of training respecting individual differences.
requirements: Issue definition first: because many question whether anything can or ought to be attempted in sex education, objectives must be carefully defined before training is planned.
constraints: The reviewed report deals rather exclusively with boys and young men; restatement for girls and young women was only contemplated.
target_learners: boys and young men (as addressed by the reviewed report)
target_learning_goals: character education addressing sexual attitudes and conduct as part of general education
examples: The American Social Hygiene Association's 1920 preliminary synthesis and integration of the returns of the sex education conference, prepared under the active direction of Dr. Thomas W. Galloway for the International Committee of Young Men's Christian Association.

article_title: Embodied word learning in schools and sustained attention in virtual reality
citation: Rudling, M., Rumetshofer, T., Nirme, J. & Mårtensson, J. (2026). Embodied Word Learning in Schools and Sustained Attention in Virtual Reality. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00395-2
title: Embodied, grounded-cognition account of L2 word learning motivating non-parasitic word-object training
description: The article frames vocabulary learning via the grounded cognition perspective, in which "language use and language learning are both embodied, ingrained in sensorimotor experience, and situated in a learning context". It contrasts L1 experiential multimodal learning with school L2 parasitic word learning, where word-object associations are weaker under the unified competition model. To mimic L1 learning the study used the ancient farming equipment paradigm, where unknown tools necessitate "a direct visual-phonological link". The theory guided the VR assembly design and the interpretation that meaningful integration of activity and language is required.
requirements: The learning activity and linguistic content must be meaningfully integrated, with the word embedded in the task itself rather than detached from it
constraints: The study's VR task introduced words only after assembly was complete, which the authors say contradicts the meaningful-integration principle and may have limited learning potential
Participants never moved beyond object form into semantic meaning
target_learners: school-aged children (Swedish middle school, years four and six, ages 9-13)
target_learning_goals: second-language (L2) vocabulary and word-object associations
examples: Children assembled segmented 3D models of old Finnish agricultural tools in VR and were shown each word in text and speech after correct assembly

article_title: Introducing students to neural communication: an embodied-learning classroom demonstration
citation: B. D. M. Hatin. (2020). Introducing students to neural communication: an embodied-learning classroom demonstration. npj Science of Learning 5:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00077-1
title: Embodied metaphor: whole-body engagement with a metaphor supports learning of abstract science concepts beyond passive engagement
description: The article frames embodied metaphors as a type of active learning especially well-suited to abstract neuroscience topics. While metaphors such as the "lock and key" metaphor for receptor activity are common, the article argues that "whole-body engagement in a learning environment supports and improves learning beyond what is observed through passive engagement with a metaphor" — e.g., acting out opening a lock with a key rather than passively hearing the metaphor. Students and foam projectiles take on roles such as soma, axon hillock, presynaptic axon terminal, post-synaptic cell, and metabotropic and ionotropic receptors.
requirements: Students physically enact the metaphor (whole-body engagement) rather than passively hearing it
constraints: Presented as especially suited to abstract topics that cannot be directly viewed, such as chemical activity at the synapse
target_learners: university students in STEM and neuroscience classrooms
target_learning_goals: understanding abstract science concepts that cannot be directly observed
examples: The article cites an earlier embodied action-potential activity in a university classroom reported to improve student understanding of the stages of an action potential.

citation: Moura, N., Vidal, M., Aguilera, A. M., Vilas-Boas, J. P., Serra, S. & Leman, M. (2023). Knee flexion of saxophone players anticipates tonal context of music. npj Science of Learning 8:22. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00172-z
title: Embodiment account: anticipatory knee movement facilitates cognitive processing and technical execution in music performance
description: The article frames knee flexion as embodiment, "the process of transforming inner subjective experiences, ideas or intentions in a physical manifestation". Within predictive coding and active inference, the authors propose that "anticipatory knee movement facilitates the cognitive processing involved in motor adaptation, and consequently supports technical execution". The framework links modeled acoustic expectations to projected movement, drawing on short-term memory models of tonal induction.
requirements: Prior familiarity with the performed piece, as participants "had previous contact with the piece".
constraints: Findings come from standard saxophone repertoire with descendant pitch lines and low rhythmical density; the authors state other musical styles and genres should be considered.

expressive music performance

title: Embodied cognition framework for physics learning
description: Embodied cognition posits that "cognitive processes are deeply rooted in the body 's interactions with the world" and that "conceptual knowledge is grounded in sensory and motor experiences". The article uses it to predict and interpret instructional-method-specific neural dynamics: active learning students preferentially engaged a somatomotor state at rest, while lecture-based students engaged visual states. The authors also invoke Hebbian learning to explain how repeated activation produces intrinsic cortical restructuring.
requirements: Instructional contexts must differ in sensorimotor versus observational engagement for the framework to predict differential neural recruitment.
constraints: The article reports it as an interpretive framework; behavioral differences between instructional groups were not observed, so neural findings did not translate to behavior.

article_title: Prior math achievement and inventive production predict learning from productive failure
citation: Manu Kapur, Janan Saba and Ido Roll. (2023). Prior math achievement and inventive production predict learning from productive failure. npj Science of Learning 8:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00165-y
title: Facilitate learning environments that give space to inventive production, since generating more solution methods promotes learning regardless of prior achievement
description: The article's pedagogical recommendation is to design PF environments that "emphasize and give more space to inventive production to encourage students to activate their prior knowledge and create more RSMs for the problems." Because the number of generated RSMs was the strongest measured predictor of learning in both topics, while prior achievement mattered little, the authors argue this emphasis "may significantly contribute to promoting math learning" for students of diverse backgrounds.
requirements: A problem-solving phase before instruction in which students can generate multiple representations and solution methods, individually or in groups
constraints: Evidence comes from two Singapore math topics (average speed, standard deviation) in schools at the high and medium end of the achievement spectrum; the authors do not claim the findings hold more generally
target_learners: Secondary mathematics students across achievement levels
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding and transfer of challenging mathematical concepts
examples: In the studies, groups designed solutions to a complex problem over two periods with no scaffolds or homework, then the teacher consolidated student-generated RSMs against canonical solutions.

article_title: Children perpetuate competence-based inequality when they help peers
citation: Sierksma, J. (2023). Children perpetuate competence-based inequality when they help peers. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00192-9
title: Empowerment vs. non-empowerment help framework
description: The article distinguishes two types of peer help: empowerment help, operationalized as hints that teach strategies, and non-empowerment help, operationalized as giving correct answers. As the article states, "Such so-called empowerment help enables the development of skills and leads to improvement in performance", whereas non-empowerment help "does not provide an opportunity to practice and improve" and "undermines feelings of autonomy and competence in recipients". The framework organizes the three studies' measures and hypotheses about who receives which type of help.
requirements: Recipients must be able to practice and use hints for skill development to occur
constraints: In this work the types were restricted to hints and answers; the article notes children might provide other types of help or none at all
target_learning_goals: skill development through practice
peer-supported learning
examples: Study 2 and 3 operationalized empowerment help as hints and non-empowerment help as correct answers in quizmaster cover-story experiments

article_title: Producing concept-motivated signs supports learning of STEM in American Sign Language
citation: Rachel Sortino, Christina Kim, Thalia Guettler, Katie McClyman, Lorna Quandt, Alicia Wooten & Rachel Pizzie. (2026). Producing concept-motivated signs supports learning of STEM content in American Sign Language. npj Science of Learning 11:37. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00418-6
title: English-motivated versus concept-motivated ASL signing styles for STEM signs
description: The article distinguishes two ASL signing styles for STEM vocabulary. English-motivated (EM) signs connect concepts through English words and "generally fall into three categories" of borrowed signs, initialized signs, and fingerspelling. Concept-motivated (CM) signs use visuospatial depiction; the article states "the iconicity of CM signing is more closely matched to the scientiﬁc or technical meaning of STEM signs". In the lessons, CM videos used three-dimensional, visuospatial depictions of content while EM videos used a more linear signing style with more fingerspelled terms. The article situates both on an embodied-learning spectrum, treating sign production by learners as more embodied than observation.
requirements: Fluent ASL signers with sufficient knowledge of ASL and STEM content to perceive the visuospatial information conveyed in CM signs
constraints: The CM style relies on more conceptual knowledge to understand the added visuospatial information in the signs, which the EM style does not
target_learners: deaf and hard of hearing (DHH) students learning STEM through ASL
target_learning_goals: STEM conceptual understanding
accessible language of instruction in ASL
examples: Study 1 created four STEM topics (acids and bases, normal distribution, graphing derivatives, stress and strain curves) as paired video lessons in both styles

article_title: Neural correlates of video game empathy training in adolescents: a randomized trial
citation: Kral, T. R. A., Stodola, D. E., Birn, R. M., Mumford, J. A., Solis, E., Flook, L., Patsenko, E. G., Anderson, C. G., Steinkuehler, C. & Davidson, R. J. (2018). Neural correlates of video game empathy training in adolescents: a randomized trial. npj Science of Learning 3:13. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0029-6
title: Design empathy training games so that engagement with empathy-specific mechanics, not generic playtime, drives the targeted learning processes
description: The article's results indicate that neural change tracked engagement with mechanics that directly target empathy processes (emotion recognition and intensity gauging), while total playtime and generically pro-social mechanics did not predict RTPJ activation change. The authors conclude that video games can improve empathy-related brain function "through skillful use of game mechanics that tap into processes underlying empathy". This supports designing mechanics around the specific underlying processes rather than relying on exposure time.
requirements: Game mechanics must directly target the processes underlying the trained skill (here, perspective taking and emotion regulation)
Telemetry or other measures of engagement with those mechanics are needed to link engagement to outcomes
constraints: The authors note additional research with clinical populations and/or participant-adaptive game difficulty is needed to elucidate whether such training leads to improvements in empathic behavior
target_learning_goals: Empathic accuracy
Perspective taking
Emotion regulation
examples: Crystals mechanics required emotion recognition, emotion intensity ratings, and empathic responding, while a taser minigame and quest completion did not predict RTPJ activation change

citation: Robert Winton, Meenam Pious & Anders Rasmussen. (2025). Training on multiple days results in better learning in embedded eyeblink conditioning in young human adults. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00347-w
title: Embedded eyeblink conditioning protocol: the US is embedded within CS duration without co-termination
description: The embedded protocol is a variant of Pavlovian conditioning in which, per the article, "the US is embedded within the duration of the CS" so that the CS and US overlap without co-terminating, unlike delay (co-terminating) or trace (stimulus-free gap) protocols. Its advantage is that learned responses can be attributed to the anticipated US onset rather than the cessation of the CS. Prior animal work cited in the article suggests it is robust to interfering intertrial USs, but its neurocognitive mechanisms in humans remain underexplored.
requirements: A CS and US whose durations overlap without co-terminating, with the US onset occurring within the CS duration
constraints: Little is known about the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying embedded eyeblink conditioning; extracerebellar regions such as the hippocampus cannot be excluded
target_learning_goals: cerebellar associative motor learning (conditioned eyeblink response acquisition)
examples: In this study a 1000 Hz, 1000 ms tone CS was paired with a corneal air puff US embedded within the CS at a 500 ms ISI, 100 trials per day across 3 non-consecutive days

It was chosen after a comparative review rated it highest in usefulness for research among low-cost EEG equipment.

Good signal from all sensors at setup

article_title: In Sync or Out of Sync? Understanding Stress and Learning Performance in Collaborative Healthcare Simulations through Physiological Synchrony and Arousal
citation: Lixiang Yan · Dragan Gašević · Vanessa Echeverria · Linxuan Zhao · Yueqiao Jin · Xinyu Li · Roberto Martinez-Maldonado. (2025). In Sync or Out of Sync? Understanding Stress and Learning Performance in Collaborative Healthcare Simulations through Physiological Synchrony and Arousal. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00475-9
title: Embodied cognition theory grounds the use of physiological indicators in embodied collaborative learning analytics
description: Embodied cognition holds that cognitive processes are deeply influenced by the body's interactions with and responses to the surrounding environment, extending learning beyond purely intellectual activity. The article uses this framework to justify collecting physiological data — heart rate, EDA, pupil dilation — during embodied collaborative learning, treating bodily responses as integral to understanding learning experiences. It further stresses that bodily experiences are socially situated, so physiological measures should be read alongside cognitive and behavioural processes in collaborative settings.

constraints: In dynamic embodied settings, frequent movement compromises EDA sensor reliability, so heart rate is preferred
Simple interpretations of heart rate are complicated by its dual autonomic regulation
target_learners: students in co-located, physically active collaborative learning environments such as healthcare simulation
target_learning_goals: understanding stress, engagement, and affective states during embodied collaborative learning
examples: The article applies the theory in high-fidelity nursing simulations where students physically interact with peers and patient manikins, modelling heart-rate synchrony and arousal with LMMs

citation: Arroyo, I., Woolf, B. P., Burelson, W., Muldner, K., Rai, D., & Tai, M. (2014). A Multimedia Adaptive Tutoring System for Mathematics that Addresses Cognition, Metacognition and Affect. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24:387–426. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0023-y
title: Emotion-phase mapping: prospective emotions in forethought, activity emotions in performance, retrospective emotions in self-evaluation
description: Combining Pekrun's control-value theory of achievement emotions with Zimmerman and Moylan's cyclical self-regulation model (forethought, performance, self-reflection), the authors propose that "prospective emotions are more likely to occur in the forethought phase, activity emotions in the performance phase, and retrospective emotions in the self-evaluation phase". This mapping guides when Wayang delivers affective and metacognitive support, on the premise that negative-valence emotions in any phase can disengage students, degrade performance and make them quit the self-regulatory loop.
requirements: A tutoring environment that detects or elicits emotions at different phases of the self-regulatory cycle
constraints: The authors state this mapping "is still an issue that deserves further investigation"
target_learners: middle and high school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: self-regulation of learning
emotional regulation during problem solving
examples: Wayang's affective learning companions and progress reports are delivered when the system infers disengagement, aiming to re-engage students in the next problem

citation: J. Leo, G. Kurdi, N. Matentzoglu, B. Parsia, U. Sattler, S. Forge, G. Donato, W. Dowling. (2019). Ontology-Based Generation of Medical, Multi-term MCQs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-00172-w
title: EMCQG: a modular ontology-based system for generating case-based medical MCQs
description: EMCQG (EMMeT Multiple Choice Question Generator) is a modular system built on EMMeT-OWL that fills question-template skeletons with content from the ontology. It comprises a templating system plus modules for stems, options, exclusions, explanations, difficulty, and question text: "the remaining main modules act as engines to fill in and structure the template skeletons with content from EMMeT-OWL". Templates encode rules over ranked clinical relations (e.g., distractor ranks must not exceed the key's), and OWL reasoning validates candidate terms against patient demographics.
requirements: A large medical ontology with clinical terms, ranked semantic relations, and POC relation attributes (EMMeT-OWL)
Expert-identified question templates representative of board-examination questions
constraints: EMCQG is not open source, and thus not available for public review
Only four medical question templates are implemented in the current version
target_learners: medical residents preparing for board examinations
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning and diagnosis
drug-of-choice and differential-diagnosis knowledge

title: EMCQG's difficulty model: question difficulty computed from stem indicativeness and distractor-key rank differences
description: EMCQG's difficulty calculator estimates question difficulty from the ranked strength of relations rather than axiomatic concept similarity. Stem indicativeness (stemInd, from sympInd and histInd) measures how strongly stem entities indicate the key; option difference (optDiff, from squared distractor differences disDiff) measures how close distractors are to the key. "The question difficulty is based on an average of the stem entities’ difficulty and the option entities’ difficulty." Squaring distractor differences weights very-similar distractors more heavily, in the absence of an empirically validated coefficient.
requirements: Ranked and POC-annotated relations in EMMeT-OWL
constraints: The authors state: "we do not provide a formal evaluation of the effectiveness of our difficulty measure"; a formal investigation of how well the models capture real difficulty is future work
target_learners: users of EMCQG generating questions for different levels of expertise
target_learning_goals: categorising generated questions as easy, medium, or hard
examples: For example question Q11, stemInd was computed as .17 and optDiff as .015, giving an overall question difficulty of .092

article_title: Effects of fear-arousing communications
citation: Janis, Irving L., and Feshbach, Seymour. (1953). Effects of Fear-Arousing Communications. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 48: 78-92.
title: Emotional-tension/reassurance account of fear appeal effectiveness
description: The authors' explanatory framework holds that a persuasive communication's overall effectiveness "will tend to be reduced by the use of a strong fear appeal, if it evokes a high degree of emotional tension without adequately satisfying the need for reassurance." It comprises two hypotheses: a strong appeal, compared with a milder one, increases the likelihood the audience is left in emotional tension not fully relieved by rehearsing the recommendations; and when strongly aroused fear is not fully relieved, the audience becomes motivated to ignore or minimize the threat. The framework explains the experiment's pattern of equal learning but poorer attitude and behavior change under the strong appeal.
requirements: The communication must contain reassuring recommendations that can potentially relieve the aroused fear for the mechanism to operate as described
constraints: The account is offered as consistent with, not proven by, the single experiment: the authors write that the evidence "appears to be consistent with" the two hypotheses

examples: The 15-minute illustrated dental hygiene lecture was prepared in three forms differing only in fear-appeal intensity, each recorded with its own set of slides and presented by the same speaker

The game supports both competitive and collaborative capture mechanics and was evaluated for usability, communication and motivation in a primary school study.

A single game level with no higher complexity levels for more skilled children

communication, coordination and collaboration skills

description: The article draws on embodied cognition theory, which holds that physical interactions and bodily cues can lighten cognitive load and improve task completion, and interest theory, which links engagement and motivation to positive learning outcomes. constraints: The cognitive theory of multimedia learning suggests sensory information in IVR could increase extraneous cognitive load and hinder learning

description: The review identifies a triadic model of empathy used in three included studies, encompassing cognitive, affective, and behavioural dimensions. Cognitive empathy refers to "understanding others’ emotions intellectually", affective empathy to "sharing and mirroring emotions", and behavioural empathy to "expressing empathy through verbal or nonverbal actions (e.g., supportive statements, gestures, or listening)". title: Embrace the human factor through synchronous and asynchronous communication in online courses
description: The article recommends that online courses deliberately incorporate the 'human' factor through broad trainer-learner and learner-learner networking via real-time messaging, online meetings, discussion forums, message boards, and emails. The article cites research showing that completely replacing classroom instruction with online instruction has negative consequences due to lack of the human factor, and that hybrid models yield more positive results.

article_title: Application of Emerging Teaching Models in Dental Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
citation: Pang Xuefei, Li Ling, Liu Xu, Wang Yan, Yang Bo. (2024). Application of Emerging Teaching Models in Dental Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. International Dental Journal. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.identj.2024.05.016
title: Taxonomy of four emerging student-centred teaching methods (PBL, CBL, TBL, FC) sharing student-centredness, group cooperation, and situational learning
description: The article organizes four emerging teaching methods — problem-based learning, case-based learning, team-based learning, and flipped classroom — by shared features and distinguishing characteristics (Table 1). All share that they "emphasize the central position of students", require students to "discuss and solve problems in small groups", and emphasize "placing learning in specific problems or case situations". They differ in orientation: PBL is problem-oriented, CBL is case-oriented using real clinical cases, TBL focuses on teamwork and communication skills, and FC is described as "a more student-centred teaching mode" requiring active participation. The review uses this taxonomy to structure its comparison against lecture-based learning.
requirements: Experimental groups must use only PBL, CBL, TBL, or FC without other educational tools, though auxiliary tools such as social media are allowed
constraints: No articles using TBL alone as the experimental teaching method were found meeting the inclusion criteria, so TBL is described but not meta-analytically evaluated
target_learners: dental undergraduates in every grade including interns
target_learning_goals: theoretical knowledge
clinical operational skills
critical thinking
self-directed learning
examples: The 29 included RCTs used PBL in 6 studies, CBL in 4 studies, FC in 16 studies, and combined methods in 3 studies

article_title: Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges
citation: Andrej Vidak, Iva Movre Šapić, Vanes Mešić, Vjeran Gomzi. (2023). Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci11110661
title: Embodied, grounded and distributed cognition accounts for AR-based physics learning
description: The review identifies embodied and grounded cognition, and distributed cognition, as theories relevant to AR-based learning. Embodied and grounded cognition holds that "cognitive activity is grounded in sensory–motor processes and situated in specific contexts and situations"; AR enables this by letting learners physically move AR markers to change the distance between simulated bodies or affect simulated meteor motion by moving through the classroom. Distributed cognition asserts that cognition is distributed across "internal human minds, external cognitive artifacts, and groups of people", so external representations such as AR visualizations facilitate learning by preventing cognitive overload in the coupled system of internal and external representations.
requirements: AR activities must couple learner bodily movement or external artifacts with the simulated content for the embodied/distributed accounts to apply.
constraints: These theories are offered as interpretive lenses for AR research rather than tested predictions within this review.
target_learners: physics students using body-tracking or marker-manipulation AR environments
target_learning_goals: learning physics through physically enacted and externally distributed representations
examples: Reviewed studies instantiate these accounts: Enyedy et al. tracked students' movements via ceiling cameras to display 3D objects, and Lindgren et al. had students impersonate meteors in a room-sized AR simulation.

title: Emotionalized dynamic assessment (EDA): dynamic assessment mediation loaded with Goleman's emotional intelligence framework

Reading comprehension in an L2
examples: Six dynamic sessions (DA1-DA5 after a baseline pretest) in which EDA learners read emotionally themed texts, answered multiple-choice items, and received mediation introducing Goleman's EI framework

Employer-visible work ethic

description: The article enumerates the design pattern used to build each lesson's electronic mind map in IMindMap: identify main and sub topics and related concepts; draw a central shape containing the text's main topic; draw colored lines outward from it, "wide at the beginning, and then curling until they are pointed at the end", with sub-ideas written atop each sub-topic; and add images and symbols that create relationships and links between ideas. Math coaches working with teachers between sessions
Guided classroom implementation of new practices

Classroom math practice change

Interactive software platform for course delivery and management
constraints: The article notes cooperative learning fails without proper structure, individual accountability, and group goals, which can turn group work into sharing answers

pronunciation

seeing alternate perspectives

title: Incorporate explicit reading strategies training into regular EFL reading instruction, even for elementary-proficiency learners
description: The article recommends that reading strategies such as predicting, text mapping, and summarizing be taught overtly as part of the normal reading syllabus rather than left to incidental use. It argues that "reading strategies training should be incorporated into regular reading instructions so that the students will acquire effective reading strategies to facilitate good comprehension", and that the strategies are "worth applying even for students of English as a foreign language with an elementary leve l of proficiency". strategic reading

article_title: "Trees Have a Soul Too!" Developing Empathy and Environmental Values in Early Childhood
citation: Lithoxoidou, L. S., Georgopoulos, A. D., Dimitriou, A. Th., & Xenitidou, S. Ch. (2017). “Trees have a soul too!” Developing Empathy and Environmental Values in Early Childhood. International Journal of Early Childhood Environmental Education, 5(1). https://naaee.org
title: Empathy development through role-taking as the developmental tool for forming ecocentric environmental values in early childhood
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that empathy is both an inherent and a social capacity that "requires cognitive achievements and therefore can be developed". Role-taking, especially affective role-taking, is the main precondition for empathic arousal; techniques such as children's literature, dramatization, anthropomorphism and inductive discussion cultivate the perspective of non-human others. Empathy toward nature is treated as a key variable for responsible environmental behavior and a vehicle for ascribing intrinsic value to non-human beings.

Developmentally appropriate techniques such as role-playing, literature and simulation games
constraints: Empathy is positioned as a tool for value formation at preschool age, not an end in itself
target_learning_goals: empathy toward non-human beings
ecocentric environmental values
pro-environmental behavior
examples: Children dressed in masks dramatized what animals and trees of the forest experience when people come by
