title: Embedding comprehension questions in video as synchronized subtitles
description: A task-design pattern in which comprehension questions appear on screen as subtitles "a few seconds before the beginning of the fragment to which they are related", remain visible during the relevant snippet, and disappear when it ends. It works for paper-and-pencil tasks, CALL and CALT prototypes, with playback controls available for learning but only play control for testing. The pilot study found no performance effect but positive attitudes.

Groups' equivalence in audiovisual comprehension could not be guaranteed

title: Employ the Multisensory Instructional Approach, or its combination with metacognitive instruction, to teach English vocabulary to underachieving L2 students

article_title: Conspicuous Strategies in Teaching Expressive Writing: A Quantitative Study Comparing Two Approaches to Process Writing
citation: Fontenot, J., Carney, K. J., & Hansen, K. (2015). Conspicuous Strategies in Teaching Expressive Writing: A Quantitative Study Comparing Two Approaches to Process Writing. Journal of Instructional Research, 4. https://jir.gcu.edu
title: Embed research-validated teaching strategies into a standard writing-process curriculum rather than replacing it
description: The article argues that a standard writing process format retains value, and that the key move is "embedding evidence-based teaching strategies into that instruction". Schools should maintain a writing curriculum with a scope and sequence, train teachers in a shared vocabulary for talking about good writing and in assessing student writing, and systematize research-validated strategies within that instruction so learners of all types can build writing skills. The study demonstrated that this element can be systematized and added to expressive-writing instruction, resulting in improved outcomes for all students.
requirements: A writing curriculum with a scope and sequence
Teacher training in a writing process, shared vocabulary for good writing, and assessment of student writing
constraints: The principle does not negate the value of a standard writing process format; it adds to it
target_learners: students of all ability types in inclusive K-8 classrooms
target_learning_goals: expressive writing proficiency
examples: The BW intervention changed instructional delivery only, not curriculum standards or expectations, and produced significant growth over the standard process writing approach

article_title: Improving At-Risk Learners' Understanding of Fractions
citation: Fuchs, L. S., Schumacher, R. F., Long, J., Namkung, J., Hamlett, C. L., Cirino, P. T., Jordan, N. C., Siegler, R., Gersten, R., & Changas, P. (2013). Improving At-Risk Learners' Understanding of Fractions. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0032446
title: Fraction instruction for at-risk learners should emphasize the measurement interpretation of fractions
description: The article's intervention centered predominantly on conceptual understanding with the major focus on the measurement interpretation of a fraction, reflecting its subordinate role in American schooling. This emphasis is in keeping with NCTM Standards and Common Core emphasis on fraction equivalence and ordering. The measurement interpretation is thought to depend on formal instruction explicating symbolic notation conventions, the inversion property, and the infinite density of fractions on the number line.
requirements: Formal instruction that explicates the conventions of symbolic notation, the inversion property of fractions, and the infinite density of fractions on any given segment of the number line
constraints: Measurement interpretation is less intuitive than part-whole understanding
target_learning_goals: understanding of fraction magnitude, equivalence, and ordering
examples: The intervention used number lines, fraction tiles, and fraction circles throughout 36 lessons, with decreasing emphasis on part-whole interpretation as lessons progressed.

citation: Hesser, T. L., & Gregory, J. L. (2016). Instructional Support Sessions in Chemistry: Alternative to Remediation. Journal of Developmental Education, 39(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1104364
title: Embedded instructional support within a college-level course as an alternative to remediation
description: A course-design pattern in which underprepared students are enrolled directly in a college-level course that embeds added instructional time and support rather than being routed into remedial courses. In this study, General Chemistry-IS covered "typical content taught in a freshman-level chemistry course" while requiring weekly 1.25-hour TA-led sessions with small groups of 12 students (maximum), focused on problem-solving practice. The pattern aligns with reform recommendations to integrate underprepared students into college-level content courses while providing additional support.
requirements: Weekly instructional sessions led by trained TAs, adding 1.25 hours to the weekly course time
TAs receive substantial training prior to the semester (a 15-hour initial training period in this study)
constraints: The study design did not permit analysis of which aspects of the treatment were effective
Applicability demonstrated at a single institution with students underprepared in math

examples: General Chemistry-IS at a single institution in Fall 2014: three sections, two instructors, 100 students enrolled, weekly sessions reinforcing lecture content with practice problems

description: The article recommends looking beyond technology designed specifically for classrooms: "the implication for teachers, and teacher educators, is to look beyond technology specifically designed for classrooms to the technology that our students choose to access away from these settings." Implementation worked through set classroom structures: 20 minutes at the beginning of each day, student responsibility for charging and packing away, goal-setting for speed and accuracy, and teacher support with mental-maths strategies. Set classroom structures and time-focussed lesson protocols are maintained
Teachers support students with mental-maths strategies, such as unpacking strategies on the board and assisting self-regulation
constraints: The mental-maths approaches in comparison classes could not be controlled, limiting generalisations

School administrators did not purchase class-sets post-intervention, possibly reflecting perceived cost-effectiveness

citation: van Hove, S., vanderhoven, E., & Cornillie, F. (2017). The tablet for Second Language Vocabulary Learning: Keyboard, Stylus or Multiple Choice. Comunicar, 50, XXV. https://doi.org/10.3916/C50-2017-05
title: Embodied cognition perspective as explanatory framework for modality effects in L2 vocabulary learning
description: The article draws on the embodied cognition perspective (Clark, 1998), which "presumes that cognition results from sensorimotor interactions with the physical environment". It explains that handwriting fundamentally influences knowledge acquisition because writing words while perceiving them being formed may facilitate learning. The authors use this framework to hypothesize that stylus writing would aid memorization, though the data only partially supported this, suggesting processing level and time on task matter more than the specific motor act.
requirements: The framework assumes that sensorimotor engagement with learning materials shapes how knowledge is acquired; applying it requires learning activities that involve bodily movement, such as writing.
constraints: The article notes previous studies most often confounded the use of technology with the act of typing; the stylus on a tablet makes it possible to distinguish the two.
The predicted handwriting advantage for memorization was not confirmed in this study.
target_learners: Secondary school pupils learning French as a second language
target_learning_goals: Memorization of L2 vocabulary lemmas
Correct spelling and use of diacritical marks in French
examples: The study hypothesized that learning French vocabulary by writing words down by means of a stylus leads to better memorization of the lemmas than typing the words on the on-screen keyboard or making multiple-choice exercises.

article_title: Mathematics-Related Competence of Early Childhood Teachers Visiting a Continuous Professional Development Course: An Intervention Study
citation: Julia Bruns, Lars Eichen, Hedwig Gasteiger. (2017). Mathematics-related Competence of Early Childhood Teachers Visiting a Continuous Professional Development Course: An Intervention Study. Mathematics Teacher Education and Development, 19(3), 76-93. MERGA.
title: EmMa – a year-long competence-oriented continuous professional development course on early mathematics education
description: EmMa (Erzieherinnen und Erzieher machen Mathematik) is a continuous professional development course for in-service early childhood teachers on early mathematics education. It comprises two introductory and four basic modules, lasts one year with a workload of approximately 100 hours, and combines presence phases (theoretical input, self-reflection, mathematical experiences) with practical phases in which teachers apply new knowledge and document children's work. constraints: The course focuses mainly on aspects of mathematical pedagogical content knowledge rather than mathematical content knowledge.

mathematical pedagogical content knowledge
beliefs towards mathematics

Congruence between learner movement and displayed anatomical content
constraints: Theoretical framework applied in a pilot context; learning gains not directly measured

embodied understanding of joint mechanics

Teacher buy-in and co-design
constraints: Universal approaches yield smaller effects than targeted ones; effects of universal interventions frequently dissipate over time

mental wellbeing
examples: The CAMH Class intervention embeds psychoeducation, reframing, grounding, movement and other ER activities directly into routine lessons across subjects

They position this combination of individual training and system safeguards as strengthening medication safety culture and reducing preventable medication-related harm.
requirements: Rolling implementation covering staff turnover, with temporary staff systematically included
Complementary system-level safeguards such as barcode scanning, which the authors call "a gold standard in medication safety"
constraints: Barcode scanning has implementation challenges and initial costs; patient engagement is limited among older patients with cognitive impairment or complex medications like opioids
target_learning_goals: Sustained adherence to safe medication administration practices
Reduction of preventable opioid administration errors
examples: The RoH was implemented on a rolling basis reaching 70% of permanent staff and has since been extended to antiparkinsonian drugs and fentanyl infusions

title: Emotional intelligence underpins communication, engagement, empathy, and self-assessment competencies of teachers
description: The review treats emotional management as part of emotional intelligence, defined as the ability to perceive, access, generate and regulate emotions to facilitate emotional and intellectual development. It reports that teachers with high emotional intelligence are self-aware, motivate themselves, deal with stress, respect and recognize students' emotions, and plan teaching environments that use emotions to enhance learning. The review concludes that the competencies of communication, motivation/engagement, empathy, preparation, organization, assessment, and self-assessment encompass aspects of emotional intelligence, positioning it as a cross-cutting underpinning of the eight competencies.

constraints: The review states that without emotional intelligence in teaching, teachers' expertise becomes less valuable, resulting in student failures — an assertion attributed to cited literature
target_learning_goals: emotionally productive teaching environments and teacher stress management

title: Emotional availability (EA) as a construct framework for assessing doctors' interactional competencies
description: Emotional availability is an established psychological construct from developmental psychology and attachment theory, encompassing "a framework of interactional qualities that enable the formation of a stable and trusted relationship". emotional attunement and responsiveness to patients' emotional signals
examples: The IC-MD coding manual rates each subscale from 1 (very problematic behaviour) to 7 (outstanding behaviour), with 5 representing a typical "good enough" performance

citation: Aliaga L, Bavolek RA, Cooper B, Mariorenzi A, Ahn J, Kraut A, Duong D, Burger C, Gisondi MA. (2024). title: Error management training mechanism account: errors focus attention on conceptual features and revise mental schemas, developing adaptive expertise
description: The article explains EMT's benefit through a mechanism account: in EMT, learners attempt problems before instruction and errors are encouraged. Specific feedback after errors, since the article notes nonspecific feedback may prevent EMT participants from fully benefiting
constraints: The article states the curriculum in its current format may not generalize to specialties beyond emergency medicine that interpret head CT scans

examples: In the trial, difficult EMT residents answered difficult questions about teaching cases before reviewing explanations, generating errors that mediated improved transfer to novel cases

citation: Chen Hao, Xuan Hanwen, Cai Jinquan, Liu Meichen, Shi Lei. (2024). The impact of empathy on medical students: an integrative review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05448-5
title: Two-component empathy framework: affective and cognitive empathy with distinct subdimensions
description: The review organizes empathy as a multidimensional construct rather than a single trait. It states that "empathy is regarded as a multidimensional construct, comprising two main components: affective and cognitive empathy." Affective empathy is "the capacity to respond emotionally to the mental states of others," divided into empathic concern and personal distress, while cognitive empathy is the capacity to understand the views or mental states of others, subdivided into perspective-taking and fantasy. This dimensional framework underpins the review's central finding that different empathy dimensions have different impacts on medical students.
requirements: Empathy must be measured with instruments that distinguish affective and cognitive components, such as the IRI or QCAE, for dimensional effects to be detected
constraints: The review notes some included studies treated empathy as a single construct, ignoring its multiple dimensions
target_learning_goals: Understanding and cultivating empathy as a multidimensional professional attribute
examples: The review analyzed burnout and depression findings separately for empathic concern, personal distress, and cognitive empathy dimensions

article_title: The impact of empathy on medical students: an integrative review.
citation: Chen Hao, Xuan Hanwen, Cai Jinquan, Liu Meichen, Shi Lei. (2024). The impact of empathy on medical students: an integrative review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05448-5
title: Empathy measurement instruments differ in population, structure, and conceptualization of empathy
description: The review describes a taxonomy of empathy measurement tools. The Jefferson Scale of Physician Empathy (JSPE/JSE) was developed for students and healthcare professionals in clinical settings and defines empathy as a cognitive attribute, whereas the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI) was "developed for the general public" and conceptualizes empathy as a combination of cognitive and affective attributes. Other tools include the Empathy Quotient, the Questionnaire of Cognitive and Affective Empathy, and the Toronto Empathy Questionnaire, mostly used with the general population. Among the 38 included articles, 21 used JSPE/JSE versions and 6 used IRI.
requirements: Choice of instrument must match the population and the empathy conceptualization relevant to the research question
constraints: The review notes differences in questionnaire usage for the same experiment may yield completely different results, an issue not addressed in the review
